# ADR-2023-150: API Service Level Agreement Revision to 99.9% Uptime

## Status
Accepted

## Date
2023-11-15

## Authors
Daniel Kim, Omar Khalil

## Context
In the grand tapestry of systems, the Helix API had been delivering freight‑forwarding data to our mid‑market partners with a 99.5 % uptime guarantee. A recent escalation from a key partner revealed intermittent downtime that exceeded this threshold, eroding confidence in our reliability promise. The incident was logged in Customer Ticket #CUST-2023-987 and sparked a Slack discussion (#api-sla-discussion) that highlighted the need for a stronger commitment. Prior ADR‑2023‑045 outlined our monitoring strategy but did not address the SLA level itself. The decision to revise the SLA was driven by the imperative to maintain partner trust and to align our contractual guarantees with the actual performance we can reliably deliver.

## Decision
Once upon a time in code, we decided to elevate the API Service Level Agreement to a 99.9 % uptime target. Let me walk you through the specifics: the new SLA will be embedded in the API documentation, and a formal communication will be sent to all partners via email and Confluence. Implementation will occur in the next release cycle, with a rollback plan that triggers if critical incidents exceed 0.1 % downtime. This threshold balances the need for resilience with operational practicality. We will also enhance our monitoring dashboards in BigQuery to provide real‑time visibility into uptime metrics, ensuring that any deviation from the target is detected and addressed promptly. 🚀

## Alternatives Considered

### Keep Existing 99.5 % SLA
We considered maintaining the status quo, but the customer escalation demonstrated that this level no longer met partner expectations, risking churn.

### Increase to 99.9 % SLA with No Rollback Plan
An alternative was to adopt the higher target without a rollback mechanism. We rejected this because it would expose the organization to unmitigated risk if the new target proved unattainable.

### Increase to 99.9 % SLA with Stricter Rollback Threshold
We also evaluated a rollback threshold of 0.05 % downtime. While more conservative, it would have delayed recovery and potentially amplified partner dissatisfaction.

## Consequences
Every line has a story: the new SLA will strengthen partner confidence and reduce escalation frequency. However, it will also increase monitoring overhead and require tighter incident response coordination. The rollback plan introduces a safety net but may trigger more frequent releases if the threshold is breached, impacting release cadence. Documentation updates will necessitate coordination between the API team and the partner enablement group.

## References
- Customer Ticket #CUST-2023-987
- Slack #api-sla-discussion
- ADR-2023-045: API Availability Monitoring

Kim's case: **(1) reassignment** (to product ops, ruled out due to lack of capacity), **(2) a voluntary early-retirement package** (ruled out as too costly), and **(3) layoff** (chosen as the most cost-effective). As Priya Singh stated in November 2023: "Cutting 15% saves $3.5M annually, which is critical for the next quarter's runway."

> **Last updated:** 2023-11-15  
> **Owner:** Daniel Kim (CTO)  
> **Status:** Stale  

## Table of Contents  
- [Overview](#overview)  
- [Decision & Rationale](#decision--rationale)

## Overview  
Once upon a time in code, a partner reached out with a legitimate concern: intermittent API downtime had slipped past our 99.5 % uptime guarantee. This incident highlighted a gap between our promise and reality, prompting a swift review of our SLA.

## Decision & Rationale  
In the grand tapestry of systems, Daniel Kim and Omar Khalil decided to elevate the API SLA to 99.9 % uptime. The new target replaces the prior 99.5 % figure and is a direct response to the recent escalation. Every line has a story, and this story is about restoring confidence and ensuring our partners feel secure in our service.

## Implementation Plan  
From the trenches of development, we will embed the new SLA in the next release cycle. A rollback plan is in place: if critical incidents exceed 0.1 % downtime, we will revert to the previous configuration. The change will be reflected in the API documentation and the Confluence space, with clear rollback procedures outlined.

## Communication & Documentation  
We will notify all partners via email and publish the revised SLA on Confluence. The API docs will be updated to include the new uptime target, rollback thresholds, and monitoring expectations. A brief FAQ will accompany the release notes to address common partner questions.

## Impact & Monitoring  
Monitoring dashboards will be adjusted to track the 99.9 % metric. Any deviation beyond the rollback threshold will trigger alerts to the incident response team and prompt an immediate review. This proactive stance ensures we catch issues before they impact partners.

## Helix Product Roadmap Pivot — TransLink Escalation

### Decision Makers
- **Maya Patel (CEO)** — primary decision-maker and initiator
- **Daniel Kim (CTO/Head of Product)** — co-approver
- **Sarah Lee (COO)** — budget/resource alignment
- **Alex Johnson / P-0001 (Compliance Lead)** — confirmed compliance rationale and joined cross-functional coordination

### Decision Date
The pivot was first formally initiated on **2023-01-15**, when Maya Patel directed Daniel Kim to abandon the B2C marketplace and redesign the freight matching engine (targeting Q3 2023). It was re-confirmed on **2023-04-05** when Hannah Lee circulated written confirmation that Maya and Daniel had approved the compliance-and-scalability-focused redesign, canceling Marco Rossi's B2C marketplace plan. The B2C roadmap was then formally removed from the product backlog on **2023-10-20** by Marco Rossi and Daniel Kim.

### Alternatives Explored
- **B2C marketplace roadmap** (Marco Rossi's original plan) — considered but rejected due to compliance gaps and inability to meet TransLink's throughput and reliability requirements
- **Phased rollout / beta pilot** — considered for the Helix Pro launch but rejected in favor of a full launch (per ART-EV-2023-125-002)
- **Manual status updates** — considered for the tracking module but replaced by an automated real-time notification system (per the 2023-05-10 meeting)

### Decisive Factor
TransLink's **critical escalation** was the trigger across all decision points. Specifically:
- The existing freight matching logic could not meet TransLink's **throughput and reliability** needs (2023-01-15)
- A **12% spike in delay reports** over the prior quarter threatened the TransLink contract (2023-05-10 meeting)
- A **data-sync failure in the shipment-tracking module** caused cascading misrouting for TransLink (2023-11-20)
- The B2C roadmap posed **compliance risks** that the compliance team confirmed would jeopardize revenue (2023-04-05)

In short, the compounding risk of losing the TransLink contract — due to reliability failures, delay complaints, and compliance gaps — drove Maya Patel and Daniel Kim to pivot resources away from the B2C marketplace and toward a full redesign of the freight-forwarding and shipment-tracking product.

# ADR-2023-150: API Service Level Agreement Revision to 99.9% Uptime

## Status
Accepted

## Date
2023-11-15

## Authors
Daniel Kim, Omar Khalil

## Context
In the grand tapestry of systems, the Helix API had been delivering freight‑forwarding data to our mid‑market partners with a 99.5 % uptime guarantee. A recent escalation from a key partner revealed intermittent downtime that exceeded this threshold, eroding confidence in our reliability promise. The incident was logged in Customer Ticket #CUST-2023-987 and sparked a Slack discussion (#api-sla-discussion) that highlighted the need for a stronger commitment. Prior ADR‑2023‑045 outlined our monitoring strategy but did not address the SLA level itself. The decision to revise the SLA was driven by the imperative to maintain partner trust and to align our contractual guarantees with the actual performance we can reliably deliver.

## Decision
Once upon a time in code, we decided to elevate the API Service Level Agreement to a 99.9 % uptime target. Let me walk you through the specifics: the new SLA will be embedded in the API documentation, and a formal communication will be sent to all partners via email and Confluence. Implementation will occur in the next release cycle, with a rollback plan that triggers if critical incidents exceed 0.1 % downtime. This threshold balances the need for resilience with operational practicality. We will also enhance our monitoring dashboards in BigQuery to provide real‑time visibility into uptime metrics, ensuring that any deviation from the target is detected and addressed promptly. 🚀

## Alternatives Considered

### Keep Existing 99.5 % SLA
We considered maintaining the status quo, but the customer escalation demonstrated that this level no longer met partner expectations, risking churn.

### Increase to 99.9 % SLA with No Rollback Plan
An alternative was to adopt the higher target without a rollback mechanism. We rejected this because it would expose the organization to unmitigated risk if the new target proved unattainable.

### Increase to 99.9 % SLA with Stricter Rollback Threshold
We also evaluated a rollback threshold of 0.05 % downtime. While more conservative, it would have delayed recovery and potentially amplified partner dissatisfaction.

## Consequences
Every line has a story: the new SLA will strengthen partner confidence and reduce escalation frequency. However, it will also increase monitoring overhead and require tighter incident response coordination. The rollback plan introduces a safety net but may trigger more frequent releases if the threshold is breached, impacting release cadence. Documentation updates will necessitate coordination between the API team and the partner enablement group.

## References
- Customer Ticket #CUST-2023-987
- Slack #api-sla-discussion
- ADR-2023-045: API Availability Monitoring

## OAuth 2.0 Migration Decision

**Decision-makers:** Daniel Kim (CTO) and Ethan Brooks (Lead Engineer) made the decision, with input from Maya Patel (Security Lead) and Luis Gomez (Platform Engineer) during a meeting.

**Date:** 2023-04-12

**Alternatives considered:**
1. **Maintaining Basic Auth with enhanced rate limiting** — rejected because it would not meet the new regulatory requirements.
2. **API Key-based authentication** — rejected because it lacked the fine-grained access control required.

**Primary motivations:**
- Compliance with new data protection regulations that required token-based authentication.
- Strengthening the overall security posture, including better audit trails, token revocation capability, and least-privilege enforcement per partner via token scopes (as noted by Maya Patel).

The decision entailed phasing out Basic Auth by Q3 2023, starting with a pilot on the shipping module, requiring all external partners to adopt OAuth 2.0 by end of quarter, updating developer docs and support training, updating the Java, Python, and Node SDKs to handle token refresh, pushing the new auth flow to the partner portal by mid-May, and enforcing OAuth 2.0 on the API gateway by end of Q3.

# ADR-2023-150: API Service Level Agreement Revision to 99.9% Uptime

## Status
Accepted

## Date
2023-11-15

## Authors
Daniel Kim, Omar Khalil

## Context
In the grand tapestry of systems, the Helix API had been delivering freight‑forwarding data to our mid‑market partners with a 99.5 % uptime guarantee. A recent escalation from a key partner revealed intermittent downtime that exceeded this threshold, eroding confidence in our reliability promise. The incident was logged in Customer Ticket #CUST-2023-987 and sparked a Slack discussion (#api-sla-discussion) that highlighted the need for a stronger commitment. Prior ADR‑2023‑045 outlined our monitoring strategy but did not address the SLA level itself. The decision to revise the SLA was driven by the imperative to maintain partner trust and to align our contractual guarantees with the actual performance we can reliably deliver.

## Decision
Once upon a time in code, we decided to elevate the API Service Level Agreement to a 99.9 % uptime target. Let me walk you through the specifics: the new SLA will be embedded in the API documentation, and a formal communication will be sent to all partners via email and Confluence. Implementation will occur in the next release cycle, with a rollback plan that triggers if critical incidents exceed 0.1 % downtime. This threshold balances the need for resilience with operational practicality. We will also enhance our monitoring dashboards in BigQuery to provide real‑time visibility into uptime metrics, ensuring that any deviation from the target is detected and addressed promptly. 🚀

## Alternatives Considered

### Keep Existing 99.5 % SLA
We considered maintaining the status quo, but the customer escalation demonstrated that this level no longer met partner expectations, risking churn.

### Increase to 99.9 % SLA with No Rollback Plan
An alternative was to adopt the higher target without a rollback mechanism. We rejected this because it would expose the organization to unmitigated risk if the new target proved unattainable.

### Increase to 99.9 % SLA with Stricter Rollback Threshold
We also evaluated a rollback threshold of 0.05 % downtime. While more conservative, it would have delayed recovery and potentially amplified partner dissatisfaction.

## Consequences
Every line has a story: the new SLA will strengthen partner confidence and reduce escalation frequency. However, it will also increase monitoring overhead and require tighter incident response coordination. The rollback plan introduces a safety net but may trigger more frequent releases if the threshold is breached, impacting release cadence. Documentation updates will necessitate coordination between the API team and the partner enablement group.

## References
- Customer Ticket #CUST-2023-987
- Slack #api-sla-discussion
- ADR-2023-045: API Availability Monitoring

## Overview  
On **March 15, 2023** (Event ID EV‑2023‑025) the Helix team decided to launch a new self‑service customer portal. The goal was to give our freight‑forwarding clients a single place to manage shipments, view analytics dashboards, and submit tickets—replacing the old manual ticketing workflow. The decision was driven by recurring customer requests for a more efficient interface that would reduce support load and improve shipment visibility.

**Participants**  
- **Nia Osei** (P‑0042) – coordinated the support integration  
- **Emily Zhao** (P‑0040) – implemented the UI components  
- **Ethan Brooks** (P‑0031) – set up the backend API and CI/CD pipeline  

## Implementation  
- **Backend**: Built a RESTful API in Node.js, deployed to our GitLab CI/CD pipeline, and exposed via the new BigQuery‑backed analytics layer.  
- **Frontend**: Emily used Adobe XD to design the UI, then hand‑off to the dev team for implementation in React.  
- **Support Integration**: Nia wired the portal to Salesforce to auto‑create tickets and sync status updates.  
- **Testing**: Fireflies.ai captured all stakeholder meetings; the transcripts were stored in Confluence for traceability.  

## Impact  
- **Client Experience**: Clients can now create, track, and close tickets directly from the portal.  
- **Support Load**: Early metrics show a 30 % drop in inbound support tickets within the first week.  
- **Analytics**: Real‑time shipment dashboards provide visibility that was previously only available via manual reports.  

## Open questions / TODOs

- Monitor API latency under peak load; consider scaling the backend if needed.  
- Gather client feedback on the UI; iterate on the design if usability issues arise.

## Product Redesign Decision for TransLink's Critical Escalation

The records show this decision unfolded in several documented stages, each building on the previous:

### Who Was Responsible
- **Maya Patel (CEO)** was the consistent primary decision-maker across all stages.
- **Daniel Kim (CTO)** co-approved the initial April redesign pivot.
- **Omar Al-Jabri (Product Lead)** co-led the November task force with Maya.

### When It Was Finalized (Key Decision Points)
1. **April 5, 2023**: Maya Patel and Daniel Kim approved a freight-forwarding product redesign focused on compliance and scalability, canceling Marco Rossi's B2C marketplace roadmap.
2. **May 10, 2023**: A formal decision was made to initiate a full redesign of the **shipment tracking module** specifically, after a 12% spike in delay reports was identified.
3. **July 5, 2023**: Maya approved a **12-week sprint cycle** using a **modular, API-first architecture**, replacing the existing monolith.
4. **November 20, 2023**: Omar and Maya convened a cross-functional task force and set a **30-day redesign deadline** after a data-sync failure caused shipment mis-routing.

### Options on the Table
- **B2C marketplace roadmap** (rejected in favor of core freight-forwarding focus)
- **Phased rollout vs. full launch** (phased rollout chosen for the November redesign for stability)
- **Monolith vs. microservices** (microservices/API-first architecture chosen per July 5 decision)
- **Feature rollback as interim fix** (approved November 20 while redesign was completed)

### Primary Reason
The core driver across all stages was **TransLink's critical escalation**: initially, compliance gaps and delay complaints (12% spike in delay reports per May 10 meeting), and later a data-sync failure causing shipment mis-routing (November 20). Maya explicitly stated on November 20: *"Numbers don't lie — this is the only viable path to regain trust."* The compliance team also confirmed on April 5 that the existing B2C roadmap posed revenue risk if the identified gaps weren't addressed.

## Shipment Tracking Module Overhaul: Key Decision Points

The records show **multiple overhaul decisions** made at different points, each with specific decision-makers, dates, alternatives, and rationales:

---

### 1. February 28, 2023 — UI Redesign Decision
**Decision-makers:** Emily Zhao, Marco Rossi, Alex Kim (Product Manager), Priya Patel (Engineering Lead)
**Finalized:** 2023-02-28; launched March 1, 2023
**Alternative reviewed:** Incremental patches to the existing UI
**Reason:** A client escalation ("Client X") exposed gaps in real-time status visibility. The team concluded incremental patches "would keep us in the same pain point," so they opted for a **full redesign** to deliver real-time status updates cleanly.

---

### 2. May 10, 2023 — Automated Notification Redesign
**Decision-maker:** Maya Patel (CEO), with data from Omar Al-Jabri
**Finalized:** 2023-05-10
**Alternative reviewed:** Continued manual status updates (status quo)
**Reason:** TransLink Logistics data showed a **23% increase in reported delays**, with 68% of incidents tied to the manual status update process (2,800 of 12,400 shipments delayed; 1,500 with no update within 24 hours). Maya decided to replace manual updates with an **automated real-time notification system**.

---

### 3. July 5, 2023 — Modular, API-First Architecture Redesign
**Decision-makers:** Maya Patel (CEO), Nia Osei (Head of Customer Success), Diego Alvarez (Product Owner/Engineering Lead)
**Finalized:** 2023-07-05
**Alternative reviewed:** Patching the existing monolithic system
**Reason:** Diego Alvarez explicitly stated the existing monolith "can't ingest real-time updates without breaking other services," and a 48-hour SLA had already been missed on a TransLink shipment due to out-of-sync tracking data. They adopted a **modular, API-first architecture** in a **12-week sprint cycle** with a dedicated cross-functional team.

---

### Summary
The most architecturally significant overhaul was finalized on **July 5, 2023** by **Maya Patel, Nia Osei, and Diego Alvarez**. The alternative of patching the monolith was rejected because it was technically incompatible with real-time data requirements. The primary driver across all decisions was recurring TransLink Logistics escalations and the inability of the legacy system to provide accurate, real-time shipment status visibility.

# Incident: Status‑Mapping Regression in Shipment Service — INC-2023-07-25-001

**Status:** Investigating  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Started:** 2023-07-25 14:12  
**Resolved:** TBD  
**Customer impact:** TransLink Logistics reported stale shipment status data; some shipments were marked as “In Transit” when they had already been delivered.  
**Incident commander:** Maya Chen (SRE Lead)

## Current understanding

A recent merge introduced a regression in the status‑mapping logic of the shipment microservice. The bug caused the service to return outdated status values for certain shipments, leading to the stale data observed by TransLink Logistics. The issue was first detected by the automated monitoring alert that flagged a spike in status‑update failures.

## Timeline (live‑updated)

- **14:12** – Alert triggered: `shipment_status_mapping_error` spike.  
- **14:13** – Maya Chen notified the support team; Nia Osei confirmed the customer’s complaint.  
- **14:15** – Initial investigation: logs show repeated `status_mapping_error` exceptions for shipment IDs 9876‑1234.  
- **14:18** – Code review identifies the recent merge of `feature/status‑fix` that altered the mapping table.  
- **14:20** – Hotfix branch `hotfix/status‑mapping‑correction` created and deployed to staging.  
- **14:25** – 30‑minute smoke test in staging: status updates now reflect correct values.  
- **14:30** – Hotfix promoted to production.  
- **14:32** – Monitoring alert cleared; status updates normal.  

## Mitigation

- Deployed hotfix to staging, performed smoke test, then promoted to production.  
- Added a new monitoring alert for `status_mapping_error` to catch future regressions early.  
- Scheduled a retrospective with the product team to review the regression and improve merge checks.

## Customer comms

- **14:14** – TransLink Logistics notified via email: “We’re aware of the status issue and are working on a fix.”  
- **14:31** – Follow‑up email: “Hotfix deployed; status data is now accurate. Let us know if you see any further issues.”

## Next update

- **14:45** – Final confirmation of resolution or any lingering anomalies.

# Incident: Shipment‑Tracking ETA Bug — INC-2023-10-01-001

**Status:** Investigating  
**Severity:** SEV-3  
**Started:** 2023-10-01 10:00  
**Resolved:** TBD  
**Customer impact:** TransLink Logistics received incorrect ETA data, leading to shipment delays and customer dissatisfaction.  
**Incident commander:** Omar Al‑Jabri  

## Current understanding

The ETA calculation logic in the shipment‑tracking module has produced erroneous values for TransLink Logistics. Initial diagnostics point to a division‑by‑zero error in the `calculate_eta` function when handling zero‑weight parcels. The issue surfaced after the recent deployment of the `v2.4.1` release.

## Timeline (live‑updated)

- 10:00 — Incident detected by automated monitoring; alert triggered for ETA anomalies.  
- 10:05 — Omar notified engineering team; incident commander assigned.  
- 10:10 — Initial log review confirms inconsistent ETA outputs for TransLink orders.  
- 10:15 — Root cause hypothesis: division‑by‑zero in ETA calculation.  
- 10:20 — Rollback of `v2.4.1` to `v2.4.0` initiated to restore baseline.  
- 10:25 — Partial rollback successful; ETA values stabilizing for new shipments.  
- 10:30 — Hotfix branch created to address division‑by‑zero; unit tests added.  
- 10:35 — Decision: The engineering team agreed to redesign the shipment‑tracking module to eliminate the ETA calculation bug, with a target delivery of the fix within 48 hours. Maya Patel approved the scope and Omar Al-.  

## Mitigation

- Rolled back to `v2.4.0` to eliminate the faulty logic from production.  
- Implemented a defensive check in `calculate_eta` to guard against zero‑weight inputs.  
- Deployed hotfix to staging; pending final validation before production rollout.  
- P-0005 (Logistics Coordinator) was consulted for impact assessment and provided input on the severity of the delay.

## Customer comms

- 10:12 — TransLink notified via email with acknowledgment of the issue and assurance of immediate action.  
- 10:30 — Updated status sent to TransLink: rollback completed, hotfix under validation.  

## Next update

- 10:45 — Awaiting staging validation results; will update by 11:00 if successful.  
- If validation fails, will revert to `v2.4.0` and investigate alternative fixes.

Subject: Strategic Decision on TransLink Freight Tracking

Hi Maya, Diego,

Once upon a time in code, we had a critical escalation from TransLink Logistics. After reviewing the incident logs and customer feedback, we decided to pivot the freight tracking module from its current batch‑update design to a real‑time dashboard that streams location data to customers. # Postmortem: Load Balancer Routing Misconfiguration — 2023-05-12

**Incident date:** 2023-05-05  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Authors:** Ethan Brooks, Daniel Kim  
**Status:** Draft  

## Summary

On May 5th, a misconfigured routing rule in our load balancer caused the Order Processing service to become unreachable. The outage impacted all inbound order traffic, leading to a temporary loss of service for our mid‑market freight‑forwarding customers. Within 15 minutes of detection, we rolled back to the last stable configuration and applied a hotfix, restoring 99.9 % uptime within 30 minutes.

## Timeline

- **09:00** — Monitoring alerts flagged a spike in 5xx errors from the Order Processing service.  
- **09:02** — Ethan Brooks identified the load balancer as the source of the issue.  
- **09:04** — Daniel Kim approved an immediate rollback to the previous stable configuration.  
- **09:05** — Rollback initiated; traffic was redirected to the stable backend pool.  
- **09:10** — Hotfix deployment began; updated routing rule pushed to the load balancer.  
- **09:25** — Configuration applied successfully; traffic routing restored.  
- **09:35** — Service health checks returned to normal; 99.9 % uptime achieved.  
- **09:40** — Incident closed; post‑mortem drafted.  

## Root cause

The root cause was a misconfigured routing rule in the load balancer that directed traffic to an unavailable backend instance. The rule was inadvertently altered during a routine update, and the change was not validated against our automated configuration checks. As a result, the Order Processing service received no traffic, leading to the observed outage.

## Contributing factors

- Lack of automated validation for load balancer configuration changes.  
- No canary deployment or staged rollout for routing rule updates.  
- Insufficient monitoring of routing table integrity.  

## What went well

- Rapid detection through automated alerts.  
- Clear communication and quick decision‑making between Ethan and Daniel.  
- Successful rollback and hotfix deployment within 15 minutes.  

## What went poorly

- The misconfiguration slipped through manual review.  
- No automated guardrails prevented the faulty rule from being applied.  

## Action items

- [ ] @Ethan: Implement automated validation scripts for load balancer configs — by 2023-06-01 [P1]  
- [ ] @Daniel: Review and update the change‑management process to include canary deployments for routing changes — by 2023-06-15 [P2]  
- [ ] @OpsTeam: Add monitoring for routing table integrity and alert on anomalies — by 2023-06-10 [P1]  

## Lessons learned

We learned that even a single misconfigured routing rule can bring an entire service offline. By adding automated validation, canary testing, and tighter monitoring, we can catch such issues before they affect customers.  

Deploying now. Let me know if you spot any issues. Thanks for the support.

# Incident: Delayed Shipment Notifications — INC-2023-10-18-001

**Status:** Investigating  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Started:** 2023-10-18 14:32  
**Resolved:** TBD  
**Customer impact:** TransLink Logistics is receiving shipment notifications up to 48 hours late, causing order‑tracking confusion and customer complaints.  
**Incident commander:** Maya Patel (Product Lead)

## Decision

Maya Patel convened an urgent cross‑functional task force to address the delayed shipment notifications reported by TransLink Logistics. The team agreed to redesign the notification pipeline, with Ni (Nia Osei) leading the redesign effort.

## Current understanding

The notification service is experiencing a latency spike due to a bug in the message queue consumer. Initial logs show a high number of `MessageAckTimeout` errors, indicating that messages are not being acknowledged within the expected window. This is causing downstream consumers to retry and ultimately delay the notification dispatch.

## Timeline (live‑updated)

- 14:32 — Incident detected by monitoring alerts on the notification service latency.  
- 14:35 — Maya convened a cross‑functional task force (Nia Osei, DevOps, Backend, P-0042).  
- 14:37 — Nia Osei started drafting a communication plan for TransLink Logistics.  
- 14:40 — Backend team identified the consumer timeout bug in the `notification_queue` consumer.  
- 14:45 — DevOps rolled back the last deployment of the consumer to the previous stable version.  
- 14:50 — Monitoring shows latency dropping but still above SLA.  

## Mitigation

- Rolled back the consumer to the last stable release.  
- Increased consumer timeout threshold temporarily to 30 s to reduce retries.  
- Restarted the consumer service to clear stale connections.  
- Updated the notification pipeline to use a new queue consumer implementation (pending code review).  

## Customer comms

- 14:38 — Nia Osei sent an email to TransLink Logistics explaining the delay and assuring a fix within 2 weeks.  
- 14:39 — TransLink Logistics acknowledged receipt of the notification.  

## Next update

- 15:00 — Re‑evaluate latency after rollback.  
- 15:30 — Deploy new consumer code if rollback does not fully resolve.  
- 16:00 — Final resolution status.

# Postmortem: Mis‑configured Load Balancer Outage — 2023-10-20

**Incident date:** 2023-10-12  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Authors:** Ethan Brooks (DevOps Engineer), Daniel Kim (Platform Engineer)  
**Status:** Final  

## Summary

On 12 Oct 2023 a 3‑hour outage of our public API was caused by a mis‑configured load balancer that failed to route traffic correctly. The outage impacted all mid‑market freight‑forwarding customers using our API for shipment tracking and rate calculations. The incident was detected by our monitoring system, escalated to the on‑call team, and resolved after traffic was rerouted and the load balancer was re‑configured.

## Timeline

- **09:00** – Monitoring alerts triggered: API latency spiked, error rate > 5 %.  
- **09:05** – On‑call engineer (Ethan) acknowledged alert, began diagnostics.  
- **09:15** – Incident escalated to platform team; Daniel joined.  
- **09:30** – Initial hypothesis: load balancer mis‑routing.  
- **10:00** – Confirmed mis‑configuration in the load balancer’s backend pool.  
- **10:15** – Traffic manually rerouted to healthy backend instances.  
- **10:30** – Load balancer re‑configured with correct backend pool.  
- **11:00** – API metrics returned to normal; error rate dropped to 0 %.  
- **12:00** – Incident closed; post‑mortem drafted.  

## Root cause

The root cause was a mis‑configured load balancer that was pointing to an outdated backend pool. The mis‑configuration caused the load balancer to route all traffic to a set of instances that were not serving the API, leading to a complete service outage. The mis‑configuration was introduced during a recent deployment of the load‑balancing layer, but no automated health checks or configuration validation were in place to catch the error before it impacted production.

## Contributing factors

- Lack of automated health checks on the load balancer configuration.  
- No configuration validation pipeline to detect incorrect backend pools.  
- Absence of a monitoring alert for mis‑configurations in the load balancer.  
- Limited visibility into the load balancer’s state during the incident.  

## What went well

- Rapid detection through existing latency and error‑rate alerts.  
- Clear communication between on‑call and platform teams.  
- Quick identification of the mis‑configuration and manual traffic rerouting.  
- Thorough documentation of the incident and root cause.  

## What went poorly

- The mis‑configuration was not caught by automated checks.  
- No alert existed for load balancer mis‑configurations, delaying detection.  
- The incident lasted 3 hours, impacting customers more than necessary.  

## Action items

- [ ] @Daniel Kim: Redesign load‑balancing layer to include automated health checks and configuration validation — by 2023-10-31 [P1]  
- [ ] @Ethan Brooks: Add monitoring alert for load balancer mis‑configurations — by 2023-10-25 [P1]  
- [ ] @Platform Ops: Update deployment pipeline to include configuration validation step — by 2023-11-07 [P2]  
- [ ] @Ethan Brooks: Deploy now and monitor for any regressions — Deploying now  

Let me know if you spot any issues. Thanks for the support.

## Adoption of the "Priority Queue" Ticket Triage System

**Date of Decision:** April 5, 2023

The decision was reached collectively by the four attendees of the Ticket Triage System Discussion meeting: **Nia Osei** (Support Lead, who drove the decision), **Diego Alvarez**, **Maya Patel**, and **Luis Gomez**. **Primary Reason for the Choice:**
The team was experiencing **weekly SLA breaches** because the existing 8-hour response window was too long, with high-priority tickets getting buried in a disorganized queue. The "Priority Queue" tool was selected because it **promised to cut response time from 8 hours to 4 hours**, which Diego noted would allow the team to hit its CSAT target. The pilot was scoped to the North America support team for two weeks, with metrics (average first response time, SLA breach rate, and CSAT) tracked in Jira and documented in Confluence.

# API Service Level Agreement Revision (SLA 99.9%)

> **Last updated:** 2023-11-15  
> **Owner:** Daniel Kim (CTO)  
> **Status:** Stale  

## Table of Contents  
- [Overview](#overview)  
- [Decision & Rationale](#decision--rationale)  
- [Implementation Plan](#implementation-plan)  
- [Communication & Documentation](#communication--documentation)  
- [Impact & Monitoring](#impact--monitoring)  
- [Open questions / TODOs](#open-questions---todos)  
- [Related](#related)

## Overview  
Once upon a time in code, a partner reached out with a legitimate concern: intermittent API downtime had slipped past our 99.5 % uptime guarantee. This incident highlighted a gap between our promise and reality, prompting a swift review of our SLA.

## Decision & Rationale  
In the grand tapestry of systems, Daniel Kim and Omar Khalil decided to elevate the API SLA to 99.9 % uptime. The new target replaces the prior 99.5 % figure and is a direct response to the recent escalation. Every line has a story, and this story is about restoring confidence and ensuring our partners feel secure in our service.

## Implementation Plan  
From the trenches of development, we will embed the new SLA in the next release cycle. A rollback plan is in place: if critical incidents exceed 0.1 % downtime, we will revert to the previous configuration. The change will be reflected in the API documentation and the Confluence space, with clear rollback procedures outlined.

## Communication & Documentation  
We will notify all partners via email and publish the revised SLA on Confluence. The API docs will be updated to include the new uptime target, rollback thresholds, and monitoring expectations. A brief FAQ will accompany the release notes to address common partner questions.

## Impact & Monitoring  
Monitoring dashboards will be adjusted to track the 99.9 % metric. Any deviation beyond the rollback threshold will trigger alerts to the incident response team and prompt an immediate review. This proactive stance ensures we catch issues before they impact partners.

## Open questions / TODOs  
- Confirm rollback thresholds with the Ops team.  
- Schedule a knowledge‑share session for partner support staff.  
- Validate the updated SLA in a staging environment before production release.

# Incident: Real‑time Tracking API Outage — INC-2023-07-12-01

**Status:** Identified  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Started:** 2023-07-12 14:00  
**Resolved:** TBD  
**Customer impact:** 12 customers experienced stale data and timeouts on the real‑time tracking API.  
**Incident commander:** Ethan Brooks  

## Current understanding

The API is timing out and returning stale data due to a race condition introduced by the new caching layer in the latest deployment. Concurrent requests are hitting the cache before it is fully populated, causing timeouts and incorrect responses.

## Timeline (live‑updated)

- 14:00 — Outage detected by monitoring; API health checks failing.  
- 14:05 — Ethan and Nia coordinate rollback to the previous stable deployment.  
- 14:10 — Hotfix applied to the API service to guard against the race condition.  
- 14:20 — Redeploy of the corrected version.  
- 14:30 — Temporary fallback endpoint enabled for affected customers.  
- 14:35 — Customer communication drafted and sent to TransLink Logistics and the other 11 customers.  

## Mitigation

- **Rollback** to the last known good deployment (successfully completed).  
- **Hotfix**: added a lock around cache population to prevent concurrent writes.  
- **Fallback**: enabled a read‑through endpoint that bypasses the cache for critical requests.  
- **Monitoring**: increased alert thresholds for API latency and error rates.  

## Customer comms

- 14:35 — Email sent to TransLink Logistics and 11 other customers explaining the outage, cause, and steps taken.  

## Next update

- By 15:00 or upon resolution.  

Deploying now. Let me know if you spot any issues. Thanks for the support.

## Authorization of the 15% Headcount Cut

### Authorizing Parties and Date
The most formally documented authorization appears in the **November 28, 2023 planning meeting** (ART-EV-2023-151-003), where four parties agreed to the cut effective **December 1, 2023**:
- **Maya Patel** (CEO)
- **Maya Chen** (CTO)
- **Alex Rivera** (HR Lead)
- **Priya Singh** (Finance Lead)

An earlier instance for the engineering team specifically was authorized by **Daniel Kim** (CTO) on **May 15, 2023**, and a further authorization for the August 2023 round was confirmed by **Aisha Patel** (HR Manager) and **Maya Patel** on **August 25, 2023** (ART-EV-2023-111-001).

### Alternatives Considered
The records are sparse on specifics. In the August 25, 2023 meeting, Maya Patel stated, *"We've considered alternatives,"* and Aisha Patel responded, *"The alternatives were not viable."* No specific alternative options are named in any record.

### Main Factor Influencing the Decision
The primary driver was a **critical customer escalation** — specifically, a client outage that cost **$1.2 million in penalties** (per the November 28 meeting notes) — which forced a product redesign and triggered cost optimization. Priya Singh further noted that a 15% cut would **save $3.5 million annually**, critical for the next quarter's financial runway.

This document outlines the proposed sales commission policy that was adopted during the December 1st strategy meeting. The policy is intended to align sales incentives with the company’s new product focus and simplified operational structure.

## Policy Details
- **Commission Rate:** Flat 12 % on all sales revenue.  
- **Scope:** Applies to all sales teams across all product lines.  
- **Effective Date:** Immediate (effective December 1, 2023).  
- **Documentation:** The policy is fully documented in Confluence for all sales teams.

The change was triggered by a critical customer escalation that exposed misaligned incentives under the previous tiered structure. # API Service Level Agreement Revision (SLA 99.9%)

> **Last updated:** 2023-11-15  
> **Owner:** Daniel Kim (CTO)  
> **Status:** Stale  

## Table of Contents  
- [Overview](#overview)  
- [Decision & Rationale](#decision--rationale)  
- [Implementation Plan](#implementation-plan)  
- [Communication & Documentation](#communication--documentation)  
- [Impact & Monitoring](#impact--monitoring)  
- [Open questions / TODOs](#open-questions---todos)  
- [Related](#related)

## Overview  
Once upon a time in code, a partner reached out with a legitimate concern: intermittent API downtime had slipped past our 99.5 % uptime guarantee. This incident highlighted a gap between our promise and reality, prompting a swift review of our SLA.

## Decision & Rationale  
In the grand tapestry of systems, Daniel Kim and Omar Khalil decided to elevate the API SLA to 99.9 % uptime. The new target replaces the prior 99.5 % figure and is a direct response to the recent escalation. Every line has a story, and this story is about restoring confidence and ensuring our partners feel secure in our service.

## Implementation Plan  
From the trenches of development, we will embed the new SLA in the next release cycle. A rollback plan is in place: if critical incidents exceed 0.1 % downtime, we will revert to the previous configuration. The change will be reflected in the API documentation and the Confluence space, with clear rollback procedures outlined.

## Communication & Documentation  
We will notify all partners via email and publish the revised SLA on Confluence. The API docs will be updated to include the new uptime target, rollback thresholds, and monitoring expectations. A brief FAQ will accompany the release notes to address common partner questions.

## Impact & Monitoring  
Monitoring dashboards will be adjusted to track the 99.9 % metric. Any deviation beyond the rollback threshold will trigger alerts to the incident response team and prompt an immediate review. This proactive stance ensures we catch issues before they impact partners.

## Open questions / TODOs  
- Confirm rollback thresholds with the Ops team.  
- Schedule a knowledge‑share session for partner support staff.  
- Validate the updated SLA in a staging environment before production release.

## Decision-Makers and Date

**Daniel Kim** and **Mei Lin** jointly concluded that the core API storage should be migrated from MongoDB to PostgreSQL. They finalized this plan on **2023-07-10**, as documented in both the meeting notes (ART-EV-2023-074-003) and the Slack thread (ART-EV-2023-074-002) from that date.

## Strategies Weighed During Planning

The following approaches were discussed:

1. **Phased vs. all-at-once migration** — They chose a phased approach, starting with read-only reporting tables first, then moving core API data in a subsequent sprint.
2. **Dual-write approach** — Writing to both databases simultaneously during cutover to verify data integrity before fully cutting over.
3. **Schema handling** — Retaining JSON columns within PostgreSQL for any remaining semi-structured data, rather than forcing a fully relational model.
4. **Migration tooling** — Using **pg_bulkload** for handling the 200 million records, and **Flyway** for schema migrations.
5. **Test migration** — Running a test migration on a staging cluster before production cutover, with a full backup beforehand.
6. **GitLab CI pipeline** — Configuring a data sync job with a built-in rollback plan.

## Main Consideration Leading to the Chosen Solution

The primary driver was **database read latency on the `/orders` endpoint**, particularly with join-heavy reporting queries. Mei Lin's profiling confirmed the bottleneck was at the database layer, and PostgreSQL testing showed query latency dropping from **350ms to 120ms** in the test environment. PostgreSQL's **indexed joins, better caching, and tighter integration with existing operational tooling** made it the clear choice over MongoDB's flexible but slower-querying document model.

# API Storage Migration Discussion — 2023-07-10

**Attendees:** Daniel Kim, Mei Lin  
**Note-taker:** Mei Lin

## Agenda

- Review current API query performance
- Discuss potential storage migration options
- Outline migration strategy and timeline

## Discussion

- **Daniel:** “We’re hitting slowdowns on the `/orders` endpoint, especially with the join-heavy reports. Mongo’s flexible schema is great, but the queries are getting sluggish.”
- **Mei:** “I’ve been profiling the API layer; the bottleneck is definitely the database read latency. PostgreSQL would give us indexed joins and better caching.”
- **Daniel:** “What about the data model? We’d need to map the document fields to relational tables.”
- **Mei:** “I’ve drafted a rough ER diagram. It’s a bit of work, but the schema is straightforward. We can keep the JSON columns for semi-structured data if needed.”
- **Daniel:** “If we go ahead, we should do it in phases to avoid downtime. Maybe start with the read‑only reporting tables first.”
- **Mei:** “Agreed. I’ll set up a migration pipeline in GitLab CI. Pipeline updated to include a data sync job and a rollback plan.”
- **Daniel:** “Let me know if you spot issues with the schema. I’ll coordinate with the devs to lock the API changes for the sprint.”

## Decisions

- **Migration to PostgreSQL**: agreed as the best path forward for faster query performance and tighter integration with existing operational tooling.
- **Phased approach**: start with read‑only reporting tables, then move core API data in the next sprint.

# API Service Level Agreement Revision (SLA 99.9%)

> **Last updated:** 2023-11-15  
> **Owner:** Daniel Kim (CTO)  
> **Status:** Stale  

## Table of Contents  
- [Overview](#overview)  
- [Decision & Rationale](#decision--rationale)  
- [Implementation Plan](#implementation-plan)  
- [Communication & Documentation](#communication--documentation)  
- [Impact & Monitoring](#impact--monitoring)  
- [Open questions / TODOs](#open-questions---todos)  
- [Related](#related)

## Overview  
Once upon a time in code, a partner reached out with a legitimate concern: intermittent API downtime had slipped past our 99.5 % uptime guarantee. This incident highlighted a gap between our promise and reality, prompting a swift review of our SLA.

## Decision & Rationale  
In the grand tapestry of systems, Daniel Kim and Omar Khalil decided to elevate the API SLA to 99.9 % uptime. The new target replaces the prior 99.5 % figure and is a direct response to the recent escalation. Every line has a story, and this story is about restoring confidence and ensuring our partners feel secure in our service.

## Implementation Plan  
From the trenches of development, we will embed the new SLA in the next release cycle. A rollback plan is in place: if critical incidents exceed 0.1 % downtime, we will revert to the previous configuration. The change will be reflected in the API documentation and the Confluence space, with clear rollback procedures outlined.

## Communication & Documentation  
We will notify all partners via email and publish the revised SLA on Confluence. The API docs will be updated to include the new uptime target, rollback thresholds, and monitoring expectations. A brief FAQ will accompany the release notes to address common partner questions.

## Impact & Monitoring  
Monitoring dashboards will be adjusted to track the 99.9 % metric. Any deviation beyond the rollback threshold will trigger alerts to the incident response team and prompt an immediate review. This proactive stance ensures we catch issues before they impact partners.

## Open questions / TODOs  
- Confirm rollback thresholds with the Ops team.  
- Schedule a knowledge‑share session for partner support staff.  
- Validate the updated SLA in a staging environment before production release.

- ADR: API Service Level Agreement Revision (ADR‑API‑SLA‑99.9)

> **Last updated:** 2023-07-25  
> **Owner:** Marco Rossi  
> **Status:** Stale  

**Event ID:** EV‑2023‑078  

## Background  
The Helix API contract has historically evolved with only backward‑compatible changes. A new feature introduced a breaking change, sparking a discussion between Marco Rossi (P‑0033) and Maya Chen (P‑0026) about how to version the API moving forward.

## Decision  
We agreed on a hybrid versioning strategy:  
- **Semantic versioning** applies **only** when a change introduces a breaking API contract.  
- All other changes are considered backward‑compatible and will be marked as **patch** or **minor** releases.

## Reason  
- Marco wanted a new major version to clearly signal the breaking change.  
- Maya preferred to keep the contract stable to avoid unnecessary disruption.  
The compromise balances clear communication of breaking changes with minimal impact on downstream consumers.

# ADR-2023-150: API Service Level Agreement Revision to 99.9% Uptime

## Status
Accepted

## Date
2023-11-15

## Authors
Daniel Kim, Omar Khalil

## Context
In the grand tapestry of systems, the Helix API had been delivering freight‑forwarding data to our mid‑market partners with a 99.5 % uptime guarantee. A recent escalation from a key partner revealed intermittent downtime that exceeded this threshold, eroding confidence in our reliability promise. The incident was logged in Customer Ticket #CUST-2023-987 and sparked a Slack discussion (#api-sla-discussion) that highlighted the need for a stronger commitment. Prior ADR‑2023‑045 outlined our monitoring strategy but did not address the SLA level itself. The decision to revise the SLA was driven by the imperative to maintain partner trust and to align our contractual guarantees with the actual performance we can reliably deliver.

## Decision
Once upon a time in code, we decided to elevate the API Service Level Agreement to a 99.9 % uptime target. Let me walk you through the specifics: the new SLA will be embedded in the API documentation, and a formal communication will be sent to all partners via email and Confluence. Implementation will occur in the next release cycle, with a rollback plan that triggers if critical incidents exceed 0.1 % downtime. This threshold balances the need for resilience with operational practicality. We will also enhance our monitoring dashboards in BigQuery to provide real‑time visibility into uptime metrics, ensuring that any deviation from the target is detected and addressed promptly. 🚀

## Alternatives Considered

### Keep Existing 99.5 % SLA
We considered maintaining the status quo, but the customer escalation demonstrated that this level no longer met partner expectations, risking churn.

### Increase to 99.9 % SLA with No Rollback Plan
An alternative was to adopt the higher target without a rollback mechanism. We rejected this because it would expose the organization to unmitigated risk if the new target proved unattainable.

### Increase to 99.9 % SLA with Stricter Rollback Threshold
We also evaluated a rollback threshold of 0.05 % downtime. While more conservative, it would have delayed recovery and potentially amplified partner dissatisfaction.

## Consequences
Every line has a story: the new SLA will strengthen partner confidence and reduce escalation frequency. However, it will also increase monitoring overhead and require tighter incident response coordination. The rollback plan introduces a safety net but may trigger more frequent releases if the threshold is breached, impacting release cadence. Documentation updates will necessitate coordination between the API team and the partner enablement group.

## References
- Customer Ticket #CUST-2023-987
- Slack #api-sla-discussion
- ADR-2023-045: API Availability Monitoring

# Postmortem: Retrospective Correction of 2023‑10‑12 API Outage Root Cause — 2024‑05‑20

**Incident date:** 2024‑05‑20  
**Severity:** SEV‑1 (high impact to internal reporting)  
**Authors:** Rajesh Kumar (P‑0005), Maya Patel (P‑0001)  
**Status:** Final  

## Summary  
On 2024‑05‑20 we amended the incident report for the 2023‑10‑12 API outage to correct the root‑cause attribution. Previously we believed a mis‑configured load balancer caused the outage; we now understand that a database schema change introduced a breaking change that was not caught by automated tests. The correction was approved by Maya Patel and Rajesh Kumar and updated across all internal documentation.

## Timeline  

- **09:00** – Maya Patel identifies a discrepancy between the 2023‑10‑12 post‑mortem and recent audit logs.  
- **09:15** – Rajesh Kumar pulls the database migration history and discovers a schema change applied on 2023‑10‑10 that removed a required column.  
- **09:30** – Investigation reveals the change was not covered by automated tests and caused the API outage.  
- **10:00** – Rajesh drafts a correction note and shares it with the incident response team.  
- **10:15** – Team reviews the evidence; consensus that the load balancer was not the root cause.  
- **10:30** – Maya Patel and Rajesh Kumar approve the correction.  
- **10:45** – Incident report for 2023‑10‑12 is updated in Confluence and the internal wiki.  
- **11:00** – Updated documentation is communicated to all stakeholders via Slack.  

## Root cause  
The root cause of the 2023‑10‑12 API outage was a database schema change that removed a column required by the API layer. The change was introduced on 2023‑10‑10 and deployed without automated regression tests covering the affected schema. Consequently, the API layer attempted to read the missing column, leading to a cascade of failures that lasted approximately three hours.

## Contributing factors  

- Lack of automated tests for database schema migrations.  
- No pre‑deployment validation step for schema changes.  
- Insufficient documentation of schema evolution in the incident response playbooks.  

## What went well  

- Rapid identification of the discrepancy by Maya Patel.  
- Clear evidence gathering and consensus building before approving the correction.  
- Transparent communication of the updated root cause to all stakeholders.  

## What went poorly  

- Initial misattribution to a load balancer mis‑configuration, which delayed the correct diagnosis.  
- Absence of automated checks for schema changes allowed the breaking change to go unnoticed.  

## Action items  

- [ ] @Rajesh Kumar: Implement automated schema migration tests in the CI pipeline — by 2024‑06‑15 [P1]  
- [ ] @Maya Patel: Update the incident response playbook to include a schema change validation step — by 2024‑06‑01 [P1]  
- [ ] @Engineering Lead: Conduct a quarterly review of all database migrations for test coverage gaps — by 2024‑07‑01 [P2]  

## Lessons learned  
This correction underscores the importance of rigorous testing for database schema changes. By embedding schema validation into our CI/CD process and updating our incident response playbooks, we can prevent similar misattributions and ensure faster, more accurate root‑cause analysis in the future.

**Who decided:** Maya Patel (CEO) and Miguel Torres (Head of Sales) made the formal decision jointly, as recorded in the meeting notes (ART-EV-2023-082-003).

# Postmortem: Load Balancer Routing Misconfiguration — 2023-05-12

**Incident date:** 2023-05-05  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Authors:** Ethan Brooks, Daniel Kim  
**Status:** Draft  

## Summary

On May 5th, a misconfigured routing rule in our load balancer caused the Order Processing service to become unreachable. The outage impacted all inbound order traffic, leading to a temporary loss of service for our mid‑market freight‑forwarding customers. Within 15 minutes of detection, we rolled back to the last stable configuration and applied a hotfix, restoring 99.9 % uptime within 30 minutes.

## Timeline

- **09:00** — Monitoring alerts flagged a spike in 5xx errors from the Order Processing service.  
- **09:02** — Ethan Brooks identified the load balancer as the source of the issue.  
- **09:04** — Daniel Kim approved an immediate rollback to the previous stable configuration.  
- **09:05** — Rollback initiated; traffic was redirected to the stable backend pool.  
- **09:10** — Hotfix deployment began; updated routing rule pushed to the load balancer.  
- **09:25** — Configuration applied successfully; traffic routing restored.  
- **09:35** — Service health checks returned to normal; 99.9 % uptime achieved.  
- **09:40** — Incident closed; post‑mortem drafted.  

## Root cause

The root cause was a misconfigured routing rule in the load balancer that directed traffic to an unavailable backend instance. The rule was inadvertently altered during a routine update, and the change was not validated against our automated configuration checks. As a result, the Order Processing service received no traffic, leading to the observed outage.

## Contributing factors

- Lack of automated validation for load balancer configuration changes.  
- No canary deployment or staged rollout for routing rule updates.  
- Insufficient monitoring of routing table integrity.  

## What went well

- Rapid detection through automated alerts.  
- Clear communication and quick decision‑making between Ethan and Daniel.  
- Successful rollback and hotfix deployment within 15 minutes.  

## What went poorly

- The misconfiguration slipped through manual review.  
- No automated guardrails prevented the faulty rule from being applied.  

## Action items

- [ ] @Ethan: Implement automated validation scripts for load balancer configs — by 2023-06-01 [P1]  
- [ ] @Daniel: Review and update the change‑management process to include canary deployments for routing changes — by 2023-06-15 [P2]  
- [ ] @OpsTeam: Add monitoring for routing table integrity and alert on anomalies — by 2023-06-10 [P1]  

## Lessons learned

We learned that even a single misconfigured routing rule can bring an entire service offline. By adding automated validation, canary testing, and tighter monitoring, we can catch such issues before they affect customers.  

Deploying now. Let me know if you spot any issues. Thanks for the support.

# Postmortem: Mis‑configured Load Balancer Outage — 2023-10-20

**Incident date:** 2023-10-12  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Authors:** Ethan Brooks (DevOps Engineer), Daniel Kim (Platform Engineer)  
**Status:** Final  

## Summary

On 12 Oct 2023 a 3‑hour outage of our public API was caused by a mis‑configured load balancer that failed to route traffic correctly. The outage impacted all mid‑market freight‑forwarding customers using our API for shipment tracking and rate calculations. The incident was detected by our monitoring system, escalated to the on‑call team, and resolved after traffic was rerouted and the load balancer was re‑configured.

## Timeline

- **09:00** – Monitoring alerts triggered: API latency spiked, error rate > 5 %.  
- **09:05** – On‑call engineer (Ethan) acknowledged alert, began diagnostics.  
- **09:15** – Incident escalated to platform team; Daniel joined.  
- **09:30** – Initial hypothesis: load balancer mis‑routing.  
- **10:00** – Confirmed mis‑configuration in the load balancer’s backend pool.  
- **10:15** – Traffic manually rerouted to healthy backend instances.  
- **10:30** – Load balancer re‑configured with correct backend pool.  
- **11:00** – API metrics returned to normal; error rate dropped to 0 %.  
- **12:00** – Incident closed; post‑mortem drafted.  

## Root cause

The root cause was a mis‑configured load balancer that was pointing to an outdated backend pool. The mis‑configuration caused the load balancer to route all traffic to a set of instances that were not serving the API, leading to a complete service outage. The mis‑configuration was introduced during a recent deployment of the load‑balancing layer, but no automated health checks or configuration validation were in place to catch the error before it impacted production.

## Contributing factors

- Lack of automated health checks on the load balancer configuration.  
- No configuration validation pipeline to detect incorrect backend pools.  
- Absence of a monitoring alert for mis‑configurations in the load balancer.  
- Limited visibility into the load balancer’s state during the incident.  

## What went well

- Rapid detection through existing latency and error‑rate alerts.  
- Clear communication between on‑call and platform teams.  
- Quick identification of the mis‑configuration and manual traffic rerouting.  
- Thorough documentation of the incident and root cause.  

## What went poorly

- The mis‑configuration was not caught by automated checks.  
- No alert existed for load balancer mis‑configurations, delaying detection.  
- The incident lasted 3 hours, impacting customers more than necessary.  

## Action items

- [ ] @Daniel Kim: Redesign load‑balancing layer to include automated health checks and configuration validation — by 2023-10-31 [P1]  
- [ ] @Ethan Brooks: Add monitoring alert for load balancer mis‑configurations — by 2023-10-25 [P1]  
- [ ] @Platform Ops: Update deployment pipeline to include configuration validation step — by 2023-11-07 [P2]  
- [ ] @Ethan Brooks: Deploy now and monitor for any regressions — Deploying now  

Let me know if you spot any issues. Thanks for the support.

# ADR-2023-150: API Service Level Agreement Revision to 99.9% Uptime

## Status
Accepted

## Date
2023-11-15

## Authors
Daniel Kim, Omar Khalil

## Context
In the grand tapestry of systems, the Helix API had been delivering freight‑forwarding data to our mid‑market partners with a 99.5 % uptime guarantee. A recent escalation from a key partner revealed intermittent downtime that exceeded this threshold, eroding confidence in our reliability promise. The incident was logged in Customer Ticket #CUST-2023-987 and sparked a Slack discussion (#api-sla-discussion) that highlighted the need for a stronger commitment. Prior ADR‑2023‑045 outlined our monitoring strategy but did not address the SLA level itself. The decision to revise the SLA was driven by the imperative to maintain partner trust and to align our contractual guarantees with the actual performance we can reliably deliver.

## Decision
Once upon a time in code, we decided to elevate the API Service Level Agreement to a 99.9 % uptime target. Let me walk you through the specifics: the new SLA will be embedded in the API documentation, and a formal communication will be sent to all partners via email and Confluence. Implementation will occur in the next release cycle, with a rollback plan that triggers if critical incidents exceed 0.1 % downtime. This threshold balances the need for resilience with operational practicality. We will also enhance our monitoring dashboards in BigQuery to provide real‑time visibility into uptime metrics, ensuring that any deviation from the target is detected and addressed promptly. 🚀

## Alternatives Considered

### Keep Existing 99.5 % SLA
We considered maintaining the status quo, but the customer escalation demonstrated that this level no longer met partner expectations, risking churn.

### Increase to 99.9 % SLA with No Rollback Plan
An alternative was to adopt the higher target without a rollback mechanism. We rejected this because it would expose the organization to unmitigated risk if the new target proved unattainable.

### Increase to 99.9 % SLA with Stricter Rollback Threshold
We also evaluated a rollback threshold of 0.05 % downtime. While more conservative, it would have delayed recovery and potentially amplified partner dissatisfaction.

## Consequences
Every line has a story: the new SLA will strengthen partner confidence and reduce escalation frequency. However, it will also increase monitoring overhead and require tighter incident response coordination. The rollback plan introduces a safety net but may trigger more frequent releases if the threshold is breached, impacting release cadence. Documentation updates will necessitate coordination between the API team and the partner enablement group.

## References
- Customer Ticket #CUST-2023-987
- Slack #api-sla-discussion
- ADR-2023-045: API Availability Monitoring

## Overview  
Once upon a time in code, a partner reached out with a legitimate concern: intermittent API downtime had slipped past our 99.5 % uptime guarantee. This incident highlighted a gap between our promise and reality, prompting a swift review of our SLA.

## Decision & Rationale  
In the grand tapestry of systems, Daniel Kim and Omar Khalil decided to elevate the API SLA to 99.9 % uptime. The new target replaces the prior 99.5 % figure and is a direct response to the recent escalation. Every line has a story, and this story is about restoring confidence and ensuring our partners feel secure in our service.

## Implementation Plan  
From the trenches of development, we will embed the new SLA in the next release cycle. A rollback plan is in place: if critical incidents exceed 0.1 % downtime, we will revert to the previous configuration. The change will be reflected in the API documentation and the Confluence space, with clear rollback procedures outlined.

## Communication & Documentation  
We will notify all partners via email and publish the revised SLA on Confluence. The API docs will be updated to include the new uptime target, rollback thresholds, and monitoring expectations. A brief FAQ will accompany the release notes to address common partner questions.

## Impact & Monitoring  
Monitoring dashboards will be adjusted to track the 99.9 % metric. Any deviation beyond the rollback threshold will trigger alerts to the incident response team and prompt an immediate review. This proactive stance ensures we catch issues before they impact partners.

The records document **multiple redesign decisions** for the shipment tracking module across 2023. The two most fully documented instances — with explicit options weighed — are:

---

### 1. February 28, 2023 (UI Redesign)

- **Decision-makers:** Alex Kim (Product Manager), Emily Zhao, Marco Rossi, and Priya Patel (Engineering Lead)
- **Exact date:** 2023-02-28 (launched 2023-03-01)
- **Options weighed:** (a) Incremental patches to the legacy UI vs. (b) full redesign of the shipment tracking UI
- **Tipping reason:** Priya argued that "incremental patches would keep us in the same pain point." Emily confirmed the mockups were ready and a full redesign could ship on March 1 and avoid another escalation. The team unanimously committed to the full rollout.

---

### 2. July 5, 2023 (Module Architecture Redesign)

- **Decision-makers:** Maya Patel (CEO), Diego Alvarez (Product Owner), and Nia Osei (Head of Customer Success)
- **Exact date:** 2023-07-05
- **Options weighed:** (a) Retaining the existing monolithic architecture vs. (b) adopting a modular, API-first architecture
- **Tipping reason:** Diego explicitly stated the current monolith "can't ingest real-time updates without breaking other services," and Nia confirmed the team had already lost a 48-hour SLA on a TransLink shipment due to out-of-sync tracking data. Maya approved the modular, API-first redesign with a confirmed 12-week sprint cycle.

---

In both cases, the decisive factor was the **inability of the existing system to deliver real-time accuracy**, made concrete by active TransLink escalations.

# Incident: Status‑Mapping Regression in Shipment Service — INC-2023-07-25-001

**Status:** Investigating  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Started:** 2023-07-25 14:12  
**Resolved:** TBD  
**Customer impact:** TransLink Logistics reported stale shipment status data; some shipments were marked as “In Transit” when they had already been delivered.  
**Incident commander:** Maya Chen (SRE Lead)

## Current understanding

A recent merge introduced a regression in the status‑mapping logic of the shipment microservice. The bug caused the service to return outdated status values for certain shipments, leading to the stale data observed by TransLink Logistics. The issue was first detected by the automated monitoring alert that flagged a spike in status‑update failures.

## Timeline (live‑updated)

- **14:12** – Alert triggered: `shipment_status_mapping_error` spike.  
- **14:13** – Maya Chen notified the support team; Nia Osei confirmed the customer’s complaint.  
- **14:15** – Initial investigation: logs show repeated `status_mapping_error` exceptions for shipment IDs 9876‑1234.  
- **14:18** – Code review identifies the recent merge of `feature/status‑fix` that altered the mapping table.  
- **14:20** – Hotfix branch `hotfix/status‑mapping‑correction` created and deployed to staging.  
- **14:25** – 30‑minute smoke test in staging: status updates now reflect correct values.  
- **14:30** – Hotfix promoted to production.  
- **14:32** – Monitoring alert cleared; status updates normal.  

## Mitigation

- Deployed hotfix to staging, performed smoke test, then promoted to production.  
- Added a new monitoring alert for `status_mapping_error` to catch future regressions early.  
- Scheduled a retrospective with the product team to review the regression and improve merge checks.

## Customer comms

- **14:14** – TransLink Logistics notified via email: “We’re aware of the status issue and are working on a fix.”  
- **14:31** – Follow‑up email: “Hotfix deployed; status data is now accurate. Let us know if you see any further issues.”

## Next update

- **14:45** – Final confirmation of resolution or any lingering anomalies.

# Postmortem: Retrospective Correction of 2023‑10‑12 API Outage Root Cause — 2024‑05‑20

**Incident date:** 2024‑05‑20  
**Severity:** SEV‑1 (high impact to internal reporting)  
**Authors:** Rajesh Kumar (P‑0005), Maya Patel (P‑0001)  
**Status:** Final  

## Summary  
On 2024‑05‑20 we amended the incident report for the 2023‑10‑12 API outage to correct the root‑cause attribution. Previously we believed a mis‑configured load balancer caused the outage; we now understand that a database schema change introduced a breaking change that was not caught by automated tests. The correction was approved by Maya Patel and Rajesh Kumar and updated across all internal documentation.

## Timeline  

- **09:00** – Maya Patel identifies a discrepancy between the 2023‑10‑12 post‑mortem and recent audit logs.  
- **09:15** – Rajesh Kumar pulls the database migration history and discovers a schema change applied on 2023‑10‑10 that removed a required column.  
- **09:30** – Investigation reveals the change was not covered by automated tests and caused the API outage.  
- **10:00** – Rajesh drafts a correction note and shares it with the incident response team.  
- **10:15** – Team reviews the evidence; consensus that the load balancer was not the root cause.  
- **10:30** – Maya Patel and Rajesh Kumar approve the correction.  
- **10:45** – Incident report for 2023‑10‑12 is updated in Confluence and the internal wiki.  
- **11:00** – Updated documentation is communicated to all stakeholders via Slack.  

## Root cause  
The root cause of the 2023‑10‑12 API outage was a database schema change that removed a column required by the API layer. The change was introduced on 2023‑10‑10 and deployed without automated regression tests covering the affected schema. Consequently, the API layer attempted to read the missing column, leading to a cascade of failures that lasted approximately three hours.

## Contributing factors  

- Lack of automated tests for database schema migrations.  
- No pre‑deployment validation step for schema changes.  
- Insufficient documentation of schema evolution in the incident response playbooks.  

## What went well  

- Rapid identification of the discrepancy by Maya Patel.  
- Clear evidence gathering and consensus building before approving the correction.  
- Transparent communication of the updated root cause to all stakeholders.  

## What went poorly  

- Initial misattribution to a load balancer mis‑configuration, which delayed the correct diagnosis.  
- Absence of automated checks for schema changes allowed the breaking change to go unnoticed.  

## Action items  

- [ ] @Rajesh Kumar: Implement automated schema migration tests in the CI pipeline — by 2024‑06‑15 [P1]  
- [ ] @Maya Patel: Update the incident response playbook to include a schema change validation step — by 2024‑06‑01 [P1]  
- [ ] @Engineering Lead: Conduct a quarterly review of all database migrations for test coverage gaps — by 2024‑07‑01 [P2]  

## Lessons learned  
This correction underscores the importance of rigorous testing for database schema changes. By embedding schema validation into our CI/CD process and updating our incident response playbooks, we can prevent similar misattributions and ensure faster, more accurate root‑cause analysis in the future.

# Incident: Real‑time Tracking API Outage — INC-2023-07-12-01

**Status:** Identified  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Started:** 2023-07-12 14:00  
**Resolved:** TBD  
**Customer impact:** 12 customers experienced stale data and timeouts on the real‑time tracking API.  
**Incident commander:** Ethan Brooks  

## Current understanding

The API is timing out and returning stale data due to a race condition introduced by the new caching layer in the latest deployment. Concurrent requests are hitting the cache before it is fully populated, causing timeouts and incorrect responses.

## Timeline (live‑updated)

- 14:00 — Outage detected by monitoring; API health checks failing.  
- 14:05 — Ethan and Nia coordinate rollback to the previous stable deployment.  
- 14:10 — Hotfix applied to the API service to guard against the race condition.  
- 14:20 — Redeploy of the corrected version.  
- 14:30 — Temporary fallback endpoint enabled for affected customers.  
- 14:35 — Customer communication drafted and sent to TransLink Logistics and the other 11 customers.  

## Mitigation

- **Rollback** to the last known good deployment (successfully completed).  
- **Hotfix**: added a lock around cache population to prevent concurrent writes.  
- **Fallback**: enabled a read‑through endpoint that bypasses the cache for critical requests.  
- **Monitoring**: increased alert thresholds for API latency and error rates.  

## Customer comms

- 14:35 — Email sent to TransLink Logistics and 11 other customers explaining the outage, cause, and steps taken.  

## Next update

- By 15:00 or upon resolution.  

Deploying now. Let me know if you spot any issues. Thanks for the support.

- Immediate rollback to the previous stable load balancer configuration.

# Postmortem: Load Balancer Routing Misconfiguration — 2023-05-12

**Incident date:** 2023-05-05  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Authors:** Ethan Brooks, Daniel Kim  
**Status:** Draft  

## Summary

On May 5th, a misconfigured routing rule in our load balancer caused the Order Processing service to become unreachable. The outage impacted all inbound order traffic, leading to a temporary loss of service for our mid‑market freight‑forwarding customers. Within 15 minutes of detection, we rolled back to the last stable configuration and applied a hotfix, restoring 99.9 % uptime within 30 minutes.

## Timeline

- **09:00** — Monitoring alerts flagged a spike in 5xx errors from the Order Processing service.  
- **09:02** — Ethan Brooks identified the load balancer as the source of the issue.  
- **09:04** — Daniel Kim approved an immediate rollback to the previous stable configuration.  
- **09:05** — Rollback initiated; traffic was redirected to the stable backend pool.  
- **09:10** — Hotfix deployment began; updated routing rule pushed to the load balancer.  
- **09:25** — Configuration applied successfully; traffic routing restored.  
- **09:35** — Service health checks returned to normal; 99.9 % uptime achieved.  
- **09:40** — Incident closed; post‑mortem drafted.  

## Root cause

The root cause was a misconfigured routing rule in the load balancer that directed traffic to an unavailable backend instance. The rule was inadvertently altered during a routine update, and the change was not validated against our automated configuration checks. As a result, the Order Processing service received no traffic, leading to the observed outage.

## Contributing factors

- Lack of automated validation for load balancer configuration changes.  
- No canary deployment or staged rollout for routing rule updates.  
- Insufficient monitoring of routing table integrity.  

## What went well

- Rapid detection through automated alerts.  
- Clear communication and quick decision‑making between Ethan and Daniel.  
- Successful rollback and hotfix deployment within 15 minutes.  

## What went poorly

- The misconfiguration slipped through manual review.  
- No automated guardrails prevented the faulty rule from being applied.  

## Action items

- [ ] @Ethan: Implement automated validation scripts for load balancer configs — by 2023-06-01 [P1]  
- [ ] @Daniel: Review and update the change‑management process to include canary deployments for routing changes — by 2023-06-15 [P2]  
- [ ] @OpsTeam: Add monitoring for routing table integrity and alert on anomalies — by 2023-06-10 [P1]  

## Lessons learned

We learned that even a single misconfigured routing rule can bring an entire service offline. By adding automated validation, canary testing, and tighter monitoring, we can catch such issues before they affect customers.  

Deploying now. Let me know if you spot any issues. Thanks for the support.
