# Postmortem: Mis‑configured Load Balancer Outage — 2023-10-20

**Incident date:** 2023-10-12  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Authors:** Ethan Brooks (DevOps Engineer), Daniel Kim (Platform Engineer)  
**Status:** Final  

## Summary

On 12 Oct 2023 a 3‑hour outage of our public API was caused by a mis‑configured load balancer that failed to route traffic correctly. The outage impacted all mid‑market freight‑forwarding customers using our API for shipment tracking and rate calculations. The incident was detected by our monitoring system, escalated to the on‑call team, and resolved after traffic was rerouted and the load balancer was re‑configured.

## Timeline

- **09:00** – Monitoring alerts triggered: API latency spiked, error rate > 5 %.  
- **09:05** – On‑call engineer (Ethan) acknowledged alert, began diagnostics.  
- **09:15** – Incident escalated to platform team; Daniel joined.  
- **09:30** – Initial hypothesis: load balancer mis‑routing.  
- **10:00** – Confirmed mis‑configuration in the load balancer’s backend pool.  
- **10:15** – Traffic manually rerouted to healthy backend instances.  
- **10:30** – Load balancer re‑configured with correct backend pool.  
- **11:00** – API metrics returned to normal; error rate dropped to 0 %.  
- **12:00** – Incident closed; post‑mortem drafted.  

## Root cause

The root cause was a mis‑configured load balancer that was pointing to an outdated backend pool. The mis‑configuration caused the load balancer to route all traffic to a set of instances that were not serving the API, leading to a complete service outage. The mis‑configuration was introduced during a recent deployment of the load‑balancing layer, but no automated health checks or configuration validation were in place to catch the error before it impacted production.

## Contributing factors

- Lack of automated health checks on the load balancer configuration.  
- No configuration validation pipeline to detect incorrect backend pools.  
- Absence of a monitoring alert for mis‑configurations in the load balancer.  
- Limited visibility into the load balancer’s state during the incident.  

## What went well

- Rapid detection through existing latency and error‑rate alerts.  
- Clear communication between on‑call and platform teams.  
- Quick identification of the mis‑configuration and manual traffic rerouting.  
- Thorough documentation of the incident and root cause.  

## What went poorly

- The mis‑configuration was not caught by automated checks.  
- No alert existed for load balancer mis‑configurations, delaying detection.  
- The incident lasted 3 hours, impacting customers more than necessary.  

## Action items

- [ ] @Daniel Kim: Redesign load‑balancing layer to include automated health checks and configuration validation — by 2023-10-31 [P1]  
- [ ] @Ethan Brooks: Add monitoring alert for load balancer mis‑configurations — by 2023-10-25 [P1]  
- [ ] @Platform Ops: Update deployment pipeline to include configuration validation step — by 2023-11-07 [P2]  
- [ ] @Ethan Brooks: Deploy now and monitor for any regressions — Deploying now  

Let me know if you spot any issues. Thanks for the support.

> **Owner:** Daniel Kim (CTO)  
> **Status:** Stale  

## Table of Contents  
- [Overview](#overview)

## Overview  
Once upon a time in code, a partner reached out with a legitimate concern: intermittent API downtime had slipped past our 99.5 % uptime guarantee. This incident highlighted a gap between our promise and reality, prompting a swift review of our SLA.

## Decision & Rationale  
In the grand tapestry of systems, Daniel Kim and Omar Khalil decided to elevate the API SLA to 99.9 % uptime. The new target replaces the prior 99.5 % figure and is a direct response to the recent escalation. Every line has a story, and this story is about restoring confidence and ensuring our partners feel secure in our service.

## Implementation Plan  
From the trenches of development, we will embed the new SLA in the next release cycle. A rollback plan is in place: if critical incidents exceed 0.1 % downtime, we will revert to the previous configuration. The change will be reflected in the API documentation and the Confluence space, with clear rollback procedures outlined.

## Communication & Documentation  
We will notify all partners via email and publish the revised SLA on Confluence. The API docs will be updated to include the new uptime target, rollback thresholds, and monitoring expectations. A brief FAQ will accompany the release notes to address common partner questions.

## Impact & Monitoring  
Monitoring dashboards will be adjusted to track the 99.9 % metric. Any deviation beyond the rollback threshold will trigger alerts to the incident response team and prompt an immediate review. This proactive stance ensures we catch issues before they impact partners.

- Confirm rollback thresholds with the Ops team.  
- Schedule a knowledge‑share session for partner support staff.

# Postmortem: Misconfigured Load Balancer Outage — 2023-02-10

**Incident date:** 2023-02-03  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Authors:** Daniel Kim, Ethan Brooks  
**Status:** Final  

## Summary  
On February 3rd, a misconfigured load balancer caused traffic to be routed to an unhealthy instance, resulting in a brief service outage for several mid‑market freight‑forwarding customers. The outage lasted approximately 30 minutes and impacted API availability. The Ops team was notified within minutes of the failure, and the incident was resolved by rolling back to the previous stable configuration, applying the corrected settings, and deploying an automated health‑check script.

## Timeline  

- **09:00** — Load balancer health‑check flag missing; traffic routed to unhealthy instance.  
- **09:05** — Ops team alerted via existing monitoring; incident opened in Jira.  
- **09:10** — Ethan Brooks identifies misconfiguration in load balancer settings.  
- **09:15** — Rollback to previous stable configuration performed.  
- **09:20** — Corrected load balancer settings applied.  
- **09:25** — Automated health‑check script deployed to monitor instance health.  
- **09:30** — New alerting rule added to notify Ops within 5 minutes of similar failure.  
- **09:35** — Service restored; API availability confirmed.  
- **09:40** — Incident closed in Jira; postmortem drafted.  

## Root cause  
The root cause was a missing health‑check flag in the load balancer configuration. Without this flag, the load balancer could not detect that the instance was unhealthy and continued to route traffic to it, leading to the outage. The absence of an automated health‑check script and an alerting rule further delayed detection and response.

## Contributing factors  

- Lack of automated health‑check script prior to the incident.  
- No alerting rule for load balancer health‑check failures.  
- Insufficient documentation of load balancer configuration requirements.  

## What went well  

- Rapid identification of the misconfiguration by Ethan Brooks.  
- Swift rollback to a known good configuration.  
- Deployment of an automated health‑check script and alerting rule within the same incident window.  

## What went poorly  

- Initial absence of a health‑check flag caused traffic to be routed to an unhealthy instance.  
- No pre‑incident monitoring or alerting for load balancer health‑check failures.  

## Action items  

- [ ] @Ethan Brooks: Implement health‑check flag in all load balancer configurations — by 2023-02-15 [P1]  
- [ ] @Daniel Kim: Deploy automated health‑check script to all instances — by 2023-02-20 [P1]  
- [ ] @Ops Team: Add alerting rule for load balancer health‑check failures, ensuring notification within 5 minutes — by 2023-02-18 [P1]  
- [ ] @QA Team: Review and update load balancer configuration documentation — by 2023-02-28 [P2]  

## Lessons learned  
This incident highlighted the critical importance of enforcing health‑check flags on load balancers and maintaining automated health‑check scripts. Proactive monitoring and alerting are essential to detect and remediate such misconfigurations before they impact customers.

Test results attached.  
Let me know if anything breaks.  
Thanks for the test plan.

# Incident: Load Balancer Mis‑config — INC-2023-04-20-01

**Status:** Investigating  
**Severity:** SEV-3  
**Started:** 2023-04-20 10:12  
**Resolved:** TBD  
**Customer impact:** API endpoints were unavailable for ~30 min, causing delayed shipment quotes for several mid‑market freight forwarders.  
**Incident commander:** Ethan Brooks  

## Current understanding

The outage began when the new deployment pushed a new container image to the staging environment. The load balancer was re‑configured to point to the new container group, but the health‑check path was incorrectly set, so the LB stopped routing traffic. This caused a 30‑minute service interruption before the traffic was manually redirected back to the previous stable version.

## Timeline (live‑updated)

- 10:12 — New container image deployed to staging.  
- 10:15 — Load balancer updated to route to new containers.  
- 10:18 — Health‑check failures detected; traffic drops to 0 %.  
- 10:20 — Ethan and Omar notice API unavailability.  
- 10:22 — Rollback initiated to previous stable image.  
- 10:25 — Traffic restored to 100 % on old containers.  
- 10:30 — Service metrics return to normal.  

## Mitigation

- Rolled back the deployment to the last stable image.  
- Updated the load balancer health‑check path to `/healthz`.  
- Restarted the LB configuration to ensure proper routing.  
- Monitored API latency and error rates; all metrics are back to baseline.  

## Customer comms

- 10:25 — Sent an internal Slack alert to the support channel.  
- 10:27 — Updated the status page with “API service restored” banner.  

## Next update

On resolution (expected 10:30). If any anomalies appear, I’ll push another update before 11:00.  

Deploying now. Let me know if you spot any issues. Thanks for the support.

# ADR-2023-150: API Service Level Agreement Revision to 99.9% Uptime

## Status
Accepted

## Date
2023-11-15

## Authors
Daniel Kim, Omar Khalil

## Context
In the grand tapestry of systems, the Helix API had been delivering freight‑forwarding data to our mid‑market partners with a 99.5 % uptime guarantee. A recent escalation from a key partner revealed intermittent downtime that exceeded this threshold, eroding confidence in our reliability promise. The incident was logged in Customer Ticket #CUST-2023-987 and sparked a Slack discussion (#api-sla-discussion) that highlighted the need for a stronger commitment. Prior ADR‑2023‑045 outlined our monitoring strategy but did not address the SLA level itself. The decision to revise the SLA was driven by the imperative to maintain partner trust and to align our contractual guarantees with the actual performance we can reliably deliver.

## Decision
Once upon a time in code, we decided to elevate the API Service Level Agreement to a 99.9 % uptime target. Let me walk you through the specifics: the new SLA will be embedded in the API documentation, and a formal communication will be sent to all partners via email and Confluence. Implementation will occur in the next release cycle, with a rollback plan that triggers if critical incidents exceed 0.1 % downtime. This threshold balances the need for resilience with operational practicality. We will also enhance our monitoring dashboards in BigQuery to provide real‑time visibility into uptime metrics, ensuring that any deviation from the target is detected and addressed promptly. 🚀

## Alternatives Considered

### Keep Existing 99.5 % SLA
We considered maintaining the status quo, but the customer escalation demonstrated that this level no longer met partner expectations, risking churn.

### Increase to 99.9 % SLA with No Rollback Plan
An alternative was to adopt the higher target without a rollback mechanism. We rejected this because it would expose the organization to unmitigated risk if the new target proved unattainable.

### Increase to 99.9 % SLA with Stricter Rollback Threshold
We also evaluated a rollback threshold of 0.05 % downtime. While more conservative, it would have delayed recovery and potentially amplified partner dissatisfaction.

## Consequences
Every line has a story: the new SLA will strengthen partner confidence and reduce escalation frequency. However, it will also increase monitoring overhead and require tighter incident response coordination. The rollback plan introduces a safety net but may trigger more frequent releases if the threshold is breached, impacting release cadence. Documentation updates will necessitate coordination between the API team and the partner enablement group.

## References
- Customer Ticket #CUST-2023-987
- Slack #api-sla-discussion
- ADR-2023-045: API Availability Monitoring

---

**Severity:** SEV-2

**Resolved:** 2023-02-03 09:45  
**Customer impact:** Service interruptions for a subset of mid‑market freight‑forwarding clients; API latency spiked and some requests failed.

- 09:30 — Health‑check script deployed to all instances.  
- 09:35 — New alerting rule added: notify Ops within 5 min of similar failure.  
- 09:45 — Traffic stabilizes; metrics return to baseline.

## Mitigation

- Rolled back to the last known good LB configuration.  
- Applied corrected settings with the required health‑check flag.  
- Deployed an automated health‑check script to all instances.  
- Added a new alerting rule to catch future misconfigurations within 5 minutes.

## Customer comms

- 09:20 — Service status page updated: “Partial outage due to load balancer issue.”  
- 09:30 — Email sent to affected clients: “We’re working on the issue; updates will follow.”  

## Next update

On resolution (09:45). Deploying now; let me know if you spot any issues. Thanks for the support.

## What the System Currently Believes

The system's **current** (post-correction) understanding is that the recommendations Ethan Brooks and Daniel Kim made on 2023-10-12 were **based on a wrong diagnosis**. At the time, they believed the outage was caused by a misconfigured load balancer (health checks never enabled, config drift during deployment). Their recommendations, recorded in ART-EV-2023-131-002, were:

1. **Redesign the load-balancing layer** to include automated health checks and configuration validation (Ethan to draft architecture doc by 2023-10-18; Daniel to review by 2023-10-23).
2. **Add a monitoring alert** to flag any config change that skips the validation step (Rajesh Singh by 2023-10-22).
3. Maya Patel was also tasked with a test plan for health-check logic by 2023-10-20.

The system now knows those recommendations were directed at the wrong problem. The actual root cause was a **database schema change applied on 2023-10-10** that removed a column required by the API layer, which was never caught by automated tests.

---

**2023-10-12** — recorded in the incident review meeting notes (ART-EV-2023-131-002).

---

**2024-05-20** — Maya Patel and Rajesh Kumar identified the discrepancy with audit logs, confirmed the schema change via database migration history, and formally amended the incident report (ART-EV-2024-155-001 and ART-EV-2024-155-003). The load balancer claim was withdrawn and documentation updated in Confluence and the internal wiki by 10:45 that day.

---

## What the System Would Have Answered on 2024-01-15

On 2024-01-15, the correction had not yet occurred (it came five months later, on 2024-05-20). The system would have reported the original, **incorrect** recommendations verbatim:

> *Ethan Brooks and Daniel Kim recommended redesigning the load-balancing layer to include automated health checks and configuration validation, and adding a monitoring alert to catch future configuration mis-matches. These recommendations arose from the conclusion that a misconfigured load balancer — specifically, health checks that were never enabled — caused the 3-hour API outage on 2023-10-12.*

# Postmortem: Retrospective Correction of 2023‑10‑12 API Outage Root Cause — 2024‑05‑20

**Incident date:** 2024‑05‑20  
**Severity:** SEV‑1 (high impact to internal reporting)  
**Authors:** Rajesh Kumar (P‑0005), Maya Patel (P‑0001)  
**Status:** Final  

## Summary  
On 2024‑05‑20 we amended the incident report for the 2023‑10‑12 API outage to correct the root‑cause attribution. Previously we believed a mis‑configured load balancer caused the outage; we now understand that a database schema change introduced a breaking change that was not caught by automated tests. The correction was approved by Maya Patel and Rajesh Kumar and updated across all internal documentation.

## Timeline  

- **09:00** – Maya Patel identifies a discrepancy between the 2023‑10‑12 post‑mortem and recent audit logs.  
- **09:15** – Rajesh Kumar pulls the database migration history and discovers a schema change applied on 2023‑10‑10 that removed a required column.  
- **09:30** – Investigation reveals the change was not covered by automated tests and caused the API outage.  
- **10:00** – Rajesh drafts a correction note and shares it with the incident response team.  
- **10:15** – Team reviews the evidence; consensus that the load balancer was not the root cause.  
- **10:30** – Maya Patel and Rajesh Kumar approve the correction.  
- **10:45** – Incident report for 2023‑10‑12 is updated in Confluence and the internal wiki.  
- **11:00** – Updated documentation is communicated to all stakeholders via Slack.  

## Root cause  
The root cause of the 2023‑10‑12 API outage was a database schema change that removed a column required by the API layer. The change was introduced on 2023‑10‑10 and deployed without automated regression tests covering the affected schema. Consequently, the API layer attempted to read the missing column, leading to a cascade of failures that lasted approximately three hours.

## Contributing factors  

- Lack of automated tests for database schema migrations.  
- No pre‑deployment validation step for schema changes.  
- Insufficient documentation of schema evolution in the incident response playbooks.  

## What went well  

- Rapid identification of the discrepancy by Maya Patel.  
- Clear evidence gathering and consensus building before approving the correction.  
- Transparent communication of the updated root cause to all stakeholders.  

## What went poorly  

- Initial misattribution to a load balancer mis‑configuration, which delayed the correct diagnosis.  
- Absence of automated checks for schema changes allowed the breaking change to go unnoticed.  

## Action items  

- [ ] @Rajesh Kumar: Implement automated schema migration tests in the CI pipeline — by 2024‑06‑15 [P1]  
- [ ] @Maya Patel: Update the incident response playbook to include a schema change validation step — by 2024‑06‑01 [P1]  
- [ ] @Engineering Lead: Conduct a quarterly review of all database migrations for test coverage gaps — by 2024‑07‑01 [P2]  

## Lessons learned  
This correction underscores the importance of rigorous testing for database schema changes. By embedding schema validation into our CI/CD process and updating our incident response playbooks, we can prevent similar misattributions and ensure faster, more accurate root‑cause analysis in the future.

# Incident: Real‑time Tracking API Outage — INC-2023-07-12-01

**Status:** Identified  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Started:** 2023-07-12 14:00  
**Resolved:** TBD  
**Customer impact:** 12 customers experienced stale data and timeouts on the real‑time tracking API.  
**Incident commander:** Ethan Brooks  

## Current understanding

The API is timing out and returning stale data due to a race condition introduced by the new caching layer in the latest deployment. Concurrent requests are hitting the cache before it is fully populated, causing timeouts and incorrect responses.

## Timeline (live‑updated)

- 14:00 — Outage detected by monitoring; API health checks failing.  
- 14:05 — Ethan and Nia coordinate rollback to the previous stable deployment.  
- 14:10 — Hotfix applied to the API service to guard against the race condition.  
- 14:20 — Redeploy of the corrected version.  
- 14:30 — Temporary fallback endpoint enabled for affected customers.  
- 14:35 — Customer communication drafted and sent to TransLink Logistics and the other 11 customers.  

## Mitigation

- **Rollback** to the last known good deployment (successfully completed).  
- **Hotfix**: added a lock around cache population to prevent concurrent writes.  
- **Fallback**: enabled a read‑through endpoint that bypasses the cache for critical requests.  
- **Monitoring**: increased alert thresholds for API latency and error rates.  

## Customer comms

- 14:35 — Email sent to TransLink Logistics and 11 other customers explaining the outage, cause, and steps taken.  

## Next update

- By 15:00 or upon resolution.  

Deploying now. Let me know if you spot any issues. Thanks for the support.

# ADR-2023-150: API Service Level Agreement Revision to 99.9% Uptime

## Status
Accepted

## Date
2023-11-15

## Authors
Daniel Kim, Omar Khalil

## Context
In the grand tapestry of systems, the Helix API had been delivering freight‑forwarding data to our mid‑market partners with a 99.5 % uptime guarantee. A recent escalation from a key partner revealed intermittent downtime that exceeded this threshold, eroding confidence in our reliability promise. The incident was logged in Customer Ticket #CUST-2023-987 and sparked a Slack discussion (#api-sla-discussion) that highlighted the need for a stronger commitment. Prior ADR‑2023‑045 outlined our monitoring strategy but did not address the SLA level itself. The decision to revise the SLA was driven by the imperative to maintain partner trust and to align our contractual guarantees with the actual performance we can reliably deliver.

## Decision
Once upon a time in code, we decided to elevate the API Service Level Agreement to a 99.9 % uptime target. Let me walk you through the specifics: the new SLA will be embedded in the API documentation, and a formal communication will be sent to all partners via email and Confluence. Implementation will occur in the next release cycle, with a rollback plan that triggers if critical incidents exceed 0.1 % downtime. This threshold balances the need for resilience with operational practicality. We will also enhance our monitoring dashboards in BigQuery to provide real‑time visibility into uptime metrics, ensuring that any deviation from the target is detected and addressed promptly. 🚀

## Alternatives Considered

### Keep Existing 99.5 % SLA
We considered maintaining the status quo, but the customer escalation demonstrated that this level no longer met partner expectations, risking churn.

### Increase to 99.9 % SLA with No Rollback Plan
An alternative was to adopt the higher target without a rollback mechanism. We rejected this because it would expose the organization to unmitigated risk if the new target proved unattainable.

### Increase to 99.9 % SLA with Stricter Rollback Threshold
We also evaluated a rollback threshold of 0.05 % downtime. While more conservative, it would have delayed recovery and potentially amplified partner dissatisfaction.

## Consequences
Every line has a story: the new SLA will strengthen partner confidence and reduce escalation frequency. However, it will also increase monitoring overhead and require tighter incident response coordination. The rollback plan introduces a safety net but may trigger more frequent releases if the threshold is breached, impacting release cadence. Documentation updates will necessitate coordination between the API team and the partner enablement group.

- Slack #api-sla-discussion
- ADR-2023-045: API Availability Monitoring

# Postmortem: Misconfigured Load Balancer Outage — 2023-02-10

**Incident date:** 2023-02-03  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Authors:** Daniel Kim, Ethan Brooks  
**Status:** Final  

## Summary  
On February 3rd, a misconfigured load balancer caused traffic to be routed to an unhealthy instance, resulting in a brief service outage for several mid‑market freight‑forwarding customers. The outage lasted approximately 30 minutes and impacted API availability. The Ops team was notified within minutes of the failure, and the incident was resolved by rolling back to the previous stable configuration, applying the corrected settings, and deploying an automated health‑check script.

## Timeline  

- **09:00** — Load balancer health‑check flag missing; traffic routed to unhealthy instance.  
- **09:05** — Ops team alerted via existing monitoring; incident opened in Jira.  
- **09:10** — Ethan Brooks identifies misconfiguration in load balancer settings.  
- **09:15** — Rollback to previous stable configuration performed.  
- **09:20** — Corrected load balancer settings applied.  
- **09:25** — Automated health‑check script deployed to monitor instance health.  
- **09:30** — New alerting rule added to notify Ops within 5 minutes of similar failure.  
- **09:35** — Service restored; API availability confirmed.  
- **09:40** — Incident closed in Jira; postmortem drafted.  

## Root cause  
The root cause was a missing health‑check flag in the load balancer configuration. Without this flag, the load balancer could not detect that the instance was unhealthy and continued to route traffic to it, leading to the outage. The absence of an automated health‑check script and an alerting rule further delayed detection and response.

## Contributing factors  

- Lack of automated health‑check script prior to the incident.  
- No alerting rule for load balancer health‑check failures.  
- Insufficient documentation of load balancer configuration requirements.  

## What went well  

- Rapid identification of the misconfiguration by Ethan Brooks.  
- Swift rollback to a known good configuration.  
- Deployment of an automated health‑check script and alerting rule within the same incident window.  

## What went poorly  

- Initial absence of a health‑check flag caused traffic to be routed to an unhealthy instance.  
- No pre‑incident monitoring or alerting for load balancer health‑check failures.  

## Action items  

- [ ] @Ethan Brooks: Implement health‑check flag in all load balancer configurations — by 2023-02-15 [P1]  
- [ ] @Daniel Kim: Deploy automated health‑check script to all instances — by 2023-02-20 [P1]  
- [ ] @Ops Team: Add alerting rule for load balancer health‑check failures, ensuring notification within 5 minutes — by 2023-02-18 [P1]  
- [ ] @QA Team: Review and update load balancer configuration documentation — by 2023-02-28 [P2]  

## Lessons learned  
This incident highlighted the critical importance of enforcing health‑check flags on load balancers and maintaining automated health‑check scripts. Proactive monitoring and alerting are essential to detect and remediate such misconfigurations before they impact customers.

- **10:00** – Confirmed mis‑configuration in the load balancer’s backend pool.  
- **10:15** – Traffic manually rerouted to healthy backend instances.  
- **10:30** – Load balancer re‑configured with correct backend pool.  
- **11:00** – API metrics returned to normal; error rate dropped to 0 %.  
- **12:00** – Incident closed; post‑mortem drafted.  

## Root cause

The root cause was a mis‑configured load balancer that was pointing to an outdated backend pool. The mis‑configuration caused the load balancer to route all traffic to a set of instances that were not serving the API, leading to a complete service outage. The mis‑configuration was introduced during a recent deployment of the load‑balancing layer, but no automated health checks or configuration validation were in place to catch the error before it impacted production.

## Contributing factors

- Lack of automated health checks on the load balancer configuration.  
- No configuration validation pipeline to detect incorrect backend pools.  
- Absence of a monitoring alert for mis‑configurations in the load balancer.  
- Limited visibility into the load balancer’s state during the incident.  

## What went well

- Rapid detection through existing latency and error‑rate alerts.  
- Clear communication between on‑call and platform teams.  
- Quick identification of the mis‑configuration and manual traffic rerouting.  
- Thorough documentation of the incident and root cause.  

## What went poorly

- The mis‑configuration was not caught by automated checks.  
- No alert existed for load balancer mis‑configurations, delaying detection.  
- The incident lasted 3 hours, impacting customers more than necessary.  

## Action items

- [ ] @Ethan Brooks: Add monitoring alert for load balancer mis‑configurations — by 2023-10-25 [P1]

# Incident: Load Balancer Mis‑config — INC-2023-04-20-01

**Status:** Investigating  
**Severity:** SEV-3  
**Started:** 2023-04-20 10:12  
**Resolved:** TBD  
**Customer impact:** API endpoints were unavailable for ~30 min, causing delayed shipment quotes for several mid‑market freight forwarders.  
**Incident commander:** Ethan Brooks  

## Current understanding

The outage began when the new deployment pushed a new container image to the staging environment. The load balancer was re‑configured to point to the new container group, but the health‑check path was incorrectly set, so the LB stopped routing traffic. This caused a 30‑minute service interruption before the traffic was manually redirected back to the previous stable version.

## Timeline (live‑updated)

- 10:12 — New container image deployed to staging.  
- 10:15 — Load balancer updated to route to new containers.  
- 10:18 — Health‑check failures detected; traffic drops to 0 %.  
- 10:20 — Ethan and Omar notice API unavailability.  
- 10:22 — Rollback initiated to previous stable image.  
- 10:25 — Traffic restored to 100 % on old containers.  
- 10:30 — Service metrics return to normal.  

## Mitigation

- Rolled back the deployment to the last stable image.  
- Updated the load balancer health‑check path to `/healthz`.  
- Restarted the LB configuration to ensure proper routing.  
- Monitored API latency and error rates; all metrics are back to baseline.  

## Customer comms

- 10:25 — Sent an internal Slack alert to the support channel.  
- 10:27 — Updated the status page with “API service restored” banner.  

## Next update

On resolution (expected 10:30). If any anomalies appear, I’ll push another update before 11:00.  

Deploying now. Let me know if you spot any issues. Thanks for the support.

## Current System Belief (as of April 10, 2024)

The system currently holds that the 2023-10-05 TransLink escalation was **not** a critical system failure requiring a technical redesign. The April 10, 2024 review (ART-EV-2024-156-003) determined via audit that the root cause was a **misconfigured routing table** — a Configuration Error. Diego Alvarez confirmed "the audit shows the root cause was a misconfigured routing table, not a system flaw," and Daniel Kim agreed to adjust the design documentation accordingly. The correct remediation was:
- Reclassify the incident as "Configuration Error"
- Add a routing-table verification step to the escalation workflow
- Issue a formal apology to TransLink Logistics

No module redesign was warranted.

---

## When the Original Account Was First Recorded

The original account — that the October 2023 escalation was caused by a **sync bug** causing a "cascade of mis-routing" requiring a full 30-day shipment-tracking module redesign and feature rollback — was first formally recorded on **2023-11-20** in the TransLink Escalation Review meeting (ART-EV-2023-127-003), attended by Omar Al-Jabri, Maya Patel, and Hannah Lee.

---

## When It Was Superseded

The original account was superseded on **2024-04-10**, when Maya Patel, Diego Alvarez, and Daniel Kim reviewed the audit findings and reclassified the incident as a Configuration Error.

---

## What the System Would Have Answered on 2023-11-15

On November 15, 2023, the November 20 escalation review meeting had **not yet occurred**. The only relevant record in existence at that date regarding the October 2023 incident was the October 5, 2023 CRM record (ART-EV-2023-122-003), which noted an escalation and a planned redesign launch in Q1 2024, but contained no specific technical decision by Diego Alvarez or Daniel Kim about the tracking module.

Therefore, on 2023-11-15, the system would have reported that **no formal technical redesign decision had yet been recorded** in response to the October 2023 TransLink escalation — only that the escalation existed and that resources had been reaffirmed toward a freight-forwarding redesign. The specific 30-day redesign/rollback decision attributed to the sync-bug diagnosis would not have been available until five days later, on November 20.

- 09:22 — Temporary routing table corrected; alert cleared.  
- 09:25 — Engineering team added routing‑table verification step to escalation workflow.  

## Mitigation

- Corrected the routing table to match production configuration.  
- Updated alert thresholds to prevent false positives.  
- Implemented a routing‑table verification step in the escalation workflow to catch similar issues early.

# Incident: Delayed Shipment Notifications — INC-2023-10-18-001

**Status:** Investigating  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Started:** 2023-10-18 14:32  
**Resolved:** TBD  
**Customer impact:** TransLink Logistics is receiving shipment notifications up to 48 hours late, causing order‑tracking confusion and customer complaints.  
**Incident commander:** Maya Patel (Product Lead)

## Decision

Maya Patel convened an urgent cross‑functional task force to address the delayed shipment notifications reported by TransLink Logistics. The team agreed to redesign the notification pipeline, with Ni (Nia Osei) leading the redesign effort.

## Current understanding

The notification service is experiencing a latency spike due to a bug in the message queue consumer. Initial logs show a high number of `MessageAckTimeout` errors, indicating that messages are not being acknowledged within the expected window. This is causing downstream consumers to retry and ultimately delay the notification dispatch.

## Timeline (live‑updated)

- 14:32 — Incident detected by monitoring alerts on the notification service latency.  
- 14:35 — Maya convened a cross‑functional task force (Nia Osei, DevOps, Backend, P-0042).  
- 14:37 — Nia Osei started drafting a communication plan for TransLink Logistics.  
- 14:40 — Backend team identified the consumer timeout bug in the `notification_queue` consumer.  
- 14:45 — DevOps rolled back the last deployment of the consumer to the previous stable version.  
- 14:50 — Monitoring shows latency dropping but still above SLA.  

## Mitigation

- Rolled back the consumer to the last stable release.  
- Increased consumer timeout threshold temporarily to 30 s to reduce retries.  
- Restarted the consumer service to clear stale connections.  
- Updated the notification pipeline to use a new queue consumer implementation (pending code review).  

## Customer comms

- 14:38 — Nia Osei sent an email to TransLink Logistics explaining the delay and assuring a fix within 2 weeks.  
- 14:39 — TransLink Logistics acknowledged receipt of the notification.  

## Next update

- 15:00 — Re‑evaluate latency after rollback.  
- 15:30 — Deploy new consumer code if rollback does not fully resolve.  
- 16:00 — Final resolution status.

## The Incident in Question: 2023-10-05 TransLink Escalation

### Which incident this is
The relevant incident is the **2023-10-05 TransLink escalation**. Nia Osei was involved in raising the TransLink shipment-tracking issues (as seen across ART-EV-2023-098-001 and ART-EV-2023-100-002), which led to **Diego Alvarez** and **Daniel Kim** being assigned action items in the subsequent review (ART-EV-2024-156-003).

---

### What the system currently believes happened
As of **2024-04-10** (ART-EV-2024-156-003), the correct account is that the 2023-10-05 incident was a **misconfigured routing table** — a configuration error — and not a critical system flaw. The incident has been formally reclassified as a **"Configuration Error."** A routing-table verification step has been added to the escalation workflow.

---

### When it first learned the original account
The original account — that the 2023-10-05 incident represented a **critical system flaw warranting a full redesign of the tracking module** — was established as early as **2023-07-05** (ART-EV-2023-098-001), when Nia Osei, Diego Alvarez, and Maya Patel decided on a modular, API-first redesign with a 12-week sprint cycle.

---

### When it learned the correction
The correction was made on **2024-04-10** (ART-EV-2024-156-003), when Diego Alvarez noted the audit showed the root cause was a misconfigured routing table, and Maya Patel concluded the correct account was a configuration error requiring a routing-table verification step — not a redesign.

---

### What it would have answered on 2023-12-15
On **2023-12-15**, the system would have stated that the 2023-10-05 TransLink escalation was a **critical flaw in core functionality** caused by a failure in the shipment-tracking module, requiring a **full modular, API-first redesign** of that module with a 12-week sprint cycle and a cross-functional team — because the correction reclassifying it as a mere configuration error did not occur until April 2024.

# Postmortem: Retrospective Correction of 2023‑10‑12 API Outage Root Cause — 2024‑05‑20

**Incident date:** 2024‑05‑20  
**Severity:** SEV‑1 (high impact to internal reporting)  
**Authors:** Rajesh Kumar (P‑0005), Maya Patel (P‑0001)  
**Status:** Final  

## Summary  
On 2024‑05‑20 we amended the incident report for the 2023‑10‑12 API outage to correct the root‑cause attribution. Previously we believed a mis‑configured load balancer caused the outage; we now understand that a database schema change introduced a breaking change that was not caught by automated tests. The correction was approved by Maya Patel and Rajesh Kumar and updated across all internal documentation.

## Timeline  

- **09:00** – Maya Patel identifies a discrepancy between the 2023‑10‑12 post‑mortem and recent audit logs.  
- **09:15** – Rajesh Kumar pulls the database migration history and discovers a schema change applied on 2023‑10‑10 that removed a required column.  
- **09:30** – Investigation reveals the change was not covered by automated tests and caused the API outage.  
- **10:00** – Rajesh drafts a correction note and shares it with the incident response team.  
- **10:15** – Team reviews the evidence; consensus that the load balancer was not the root cause.  
- **10:30** – Maya Patel and Rajesh Kumar approve the correction.  
- **10:45** – Incident report for 2023‑10‑12 is updated in Confluence and the internal wiki.  
- **11:00** – Updated documentation is communicated to all stakeholders via Slack.  

## Root cause  
The root cause of the 2023‑10‑12 API outage was a database schema change that removed a column required by the API layer. The change was introduced on 2023‑10‑10 and deployed without automated regression tests covering the affected schema. Consequently, the API layer attempted to read the missing column, leading to a cascade of failures that lasted approximately three hours.

## Contributing factors  

- Lack of automated tests for database schema migrations.  
- No pre‑deployment validation step for schema changes.  
- Insufficient documentation of schema evolution in the incident response playbooks.  

## What went well  

- Rapid identification of the discrepancy by Maya Patel.  
- Clear evidence gathering and consensus building before approving the correction.  
- Transparent communication of the updated root cause to all stakeholders.  

## What went poorly  

- Initial misattribution to a load balancer mis‑configuration, which delayed the correct diagnosis.  
- Absence of automated checks for schema changes allowed the breaking change to go unnoticed.  

## Action items  

- [ ] @Rajesh Kumar: Implement automated schema migration tests in the CI pipeline — by 2024‑06‑15 [P1]  
- [ ] @Maya Patel: Update the incident response playbook to include a schema change validation step — by 2024‑06‑01 [P1]  
- [ ] @Engineering Lead: Conduct a quarterly review of all database migrations for test coverage gaps — by 2024‑07‑01 [P2]  

## Lessons learned  
This correction underscores the importance of rigorous testing for database schema changes. By embedding schema validation into our CI/CD process and updating our incident response playbooks, we can prevent similar misattributions and ensure faster, more accurate root‑cause analysis in the future.

# Incident: Accidental S3 Bucket Exposure — INC-2023-02-28-01

**Status:** Resolved  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Started:** 2023-02-28 09:12  
**Resolved:** 2023-02-28 11:05  
**Customer impact:** Customer contact data exposed for ~2 hours; no external notification required.  
**Incident commander:** Omar Al‑Jabri  

## Current understanding

An S3 bucket that stores customer contact data was misconfigured to be publicly readable. The exposure was detected when Ethan Brooks noticed anomalous traffic patterns and reported it immediately. The incident was contained within 2 hours after isolation and patching.

## Timeline (live‑updated)

- **09:12** – Ethan Brooks identifies anomalous S3 access logs and reports to Omar.  
- **09:15** – Omar convenes the incident response team.  
- **09:20** – Team isolates the affected database and revokes compromised IAM credentials.  
- **09:35** – Patch applied to S3 bucket policy to enforce private access.  
- **10:00** – Full audit of access logs initiated.  
- **10:45** – Verification that no further public reads are possible.  
- **11:05** – Incident marked resolved; no external notification required.

## Mitigation

- **Isolation:** The database containing exposed data was taken offline to prevent further reads.  
- **Credential revocation:** All IAM roles with access to the bucket were revoked and rotated.  
- **Policy patch:** Updated the bucket policy to `BlockPublicAcls` and `IgnorePublicAcls` and enabled `BucketPolicyOnly`.  
- **Audit:** Scheduled a comprehensive audit of all S3 buckets and IAM policies.  

## Customer comms

- No external notification required at this time.  
- Internal stakeholders notified via Slack channel #incident‑response.

## Next update

On resolution (already provided).

**Status:** Investigating  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Started:** 2023-11-15 09:12  
**Resolved:** TBD  
**Customer impact:** Sales portal intermittently unreachable for ~45 min.  
**Incident commander:** Maya Patel  

## Current understanding

The sales portal is down due to a mis‑configured load‑balancer rule that caused traffic to be routed to an inactive backend. Initial diagnostics show that the rule was added during a recent deployment but the change was not validated against the firewall policy. We are rolling back the rule to restore service.

## Timeline (live‑updated)

- 09:12 — Incident detected via monitoring alerts.  
- 09:15 — Maya Patel notified; incident commander assigned.  
- 09:18 — Load‑balancer logs show traffic to non‑existent backend.  
- 09:20 — Rollback of the recent rule initiated.  
- 09:25 — Traffic restored to default routing; portal back online.  
- 09:30 — Nia Osei confirms service availability with end‑users.  
- 09:35 — Incident logged in the incident report system.  

## Mitigation

- Rolled back the recent load‑balancer rule to default routing.  
- Verified backend health checks; all services operational.  
- Updated firewall rule to block mis‑configured traffic patterns.  

## Customer comms

- 09:22 — Email sent to affected customers: “Sales portal experiencing intermittent downtime; we are working to resolve.”  
- 09:26 — Status page updated with live progress.  

## Next update

- 09:45 — Re‑run health checks; confirm no residual issues.  
- 10:00 — Final resolution confirmation and post‑mortem kickoff.  

---

### Retrospective Note (as of 2024-06-15)

Previously we believed that the 2023‑11‑15 outage was caused solely by a mis‑configured load‑balancer rule, and that the rollback restored service within 45 minutes. We now understand that the root cause was a mis‑configured firewall rule that was not captured in the original documentation. Maya Patel and the CTO reviewed the audit findings and decided to correct the incident documentation, update the knowledge graph entry for the 2023‑11‑15 outage, and revise the firewall rule change process to include automated validation. They also added a new monitoring rule to detect misconfigurations before they affect the sales portal.

# Incident: Delayed Shipment Notifications — INC-2023-10-18-001

**Status:** Investigating  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Started:** 2023-10-18 14:32  
**Resolved:** TBD  
**Customer impact:** TransLink Logistics is receiving shipment notifications up to 48 hours late, causing order‑tracking confusion and customer complaints.  
**Incident commander:** Maya Patel (Product Lead)

## Decision

Maya Patel convened an urgent cross‑functional task force to address the delayed shipment notifications reported by TransLink Logistics. The team agreed to redesign the notification pipeline, with Ni (Nia Osei) leading the redesign effort.

## Current understanding

The notification service is experiencing a latency spike due to a bug in the message queue consumer. Initial logs show a high number of `MessageAckTimeout` errors, indicating that messages are not being acknowledged within the expected window. This is causing downstream consumers to retry and ultimately delay the notification dispatch.

## Timeline (live‑updated)

- 14:32 — Incident detected by monitoring alerts on the notification service latency.  
- 14:35 — Maya convened a cross‑functional task force (Nia Osei, DevOps, Backend, P-0042).  
- 14:37 — Nia Osei started drafting a communication plan for TransLink Logistics.  
- 14:40 — Backend team identified the consumer timeout bug in the `notification_queue` consumer.  
- 14:45 — DevOps rolled back the last deployment of the consumer to the previous stable version.  
- 14:50 — Monitoring shows latency dropping but still above SLA.  

## Mitigation

- Rolled back the consumer to the last stable release.  
- Increased consumer timeout threshold temporarily to 30 s to reduce retries.  
- Restarted the consumer service to clear stale connections.  
- Updated the notification pipeline to use a new queue consumer implementation (pending code review).  

## Customer comms

- 14:38 — Nia Osei sent an email to TransLink Logistics explaining the delay and assuring a fix within 2 weeks.  
- 14:39 — TransLink Logistics acknowledged receipt of the notification.  

## Next update

- 15:00 — Re‑evaluate latency after rollback.  
- 15:30 — Deploy new consumer code if rollback does not fully resolve.  
- 16:00 — Final resolution status.

## The 3-Hour Outage Examined by Ethan Brooks and Daniel Kim

### The Incident
This is the **2023-10-12 outage** documented in postmortem **ART-EV-2023-131-001** (postmortem written 2023-10-20, incident date 2023-10-12), authored by Ethan Brooks (DevOps Engineer) and Daniel Kim (Platform Engineer).

---

### First Explanation (recorded 2023-10-20)
The root cause was **a mis-configured load balancer pointing to an outdated backend pool**, introduced during a recent deployment of the load-balancing layer. No automated health checks or configuration validation were in place to catch the error before it hit production, causing a complete 3-hour service outage for all mid-market freight-forwarding customers.

---

### Updated Explanation
The postmortem itself contains a cross-reference noting it was **"(retroactively_corrected_by) See meeting transcript ART-EV-2024-155-001 for the corrected root-cause analysis."** However, **ART-EV-2024-155-001 is not present in the retrieved records**, so the specific corrected explanation for this incident cannot be confirmed from the available documents. (Note: ART-EV-2024-154-001, dated 2024-06-15, corrects the root cause of the *2023-11-15* outage to a firewall misconfiguration, but that is a different incident.)

---

### What the System Would Have Said on 2023-12-01
On 2023-12-01, only the original postmortem (ART-EV-2023-131-001) would have been in effect. The system would have answered: **the outage was caused by a mis-configured load balancer pointing to an outdated backend pool**, introduced during a recent deployment, with no automated health checks or validation pipeline to catch it.

---

### Summary
- **First explanation recorded:** 2023-10-20 — load balancer mis-configuration (outdated backend pool)
- **Updated explanation added:** Referenced as existing (via ART-EV-2024-155-001), but that document is not in the retrieved records; the correction cannot be specified
- **Answer on 2023-12-01:** Load balancer mis-configuration pointing to an outdated backend pool

# Postmortem: Misconfigured Load Balancer Outage — 2023-02-10

**Incident date:** 2023-02-03  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Authors:** Daniel Kim, Ethan Brooks  
**Status:** Final  

## Summary  
On February 3rd, a misconfigured load balancer caused traffic to be routed to an unhealthy instance, resulting in a brief service outage for several mid‑market freight‑forwarding customers. The outage lasted approximately 30 minutes and impacted API availability. The Ops team was notified within minutes of the failure, and the incident was resolved by rolling back to the previous stable configuration, applying the corrected settings, and deploying an automated health‑check script.

## Timeline  

- **09:00** — Load balancer health‑check flag missing; traffic routed to unhealthy instance.  
- **09:05** — Ops team alerted via existing monitoring; incident opened in Jira.  
- **09:10** — Ethan Brooks identifies misconfiguration in load balancer settings.  
- **09:15** — Rollback to previous stable configuration performed.  
- **09:20** — Corrected load balancer settings applied.  
- **09:25** — Automated health‑check script deployed to monitor instance health.  
- **09:30** — New alerting rule added to notify Ops within 5 minutes of similar failure.  
- **09:35** — Service restored; API availability confirmed.  
- **09:40** — Incident closed in Jira; postmortem drafted.  

## Root cause  
The root cause was a missing health‑check flag in the load balancer configuration. Without this flag, the load balancer could not detect that the instance was unhealthy and continued to route traffic to it, leading to the outage. The absence of an automated health‑check script and an alerting rule further delayed detection and response.

## Contributing factors  

- Lack of automated health‑check script prior to the incident.  
- No alerting rule for load balancer health‑check failures.  
- Insufficient documentation of load balancer configuration requirements.  

## What went well  

- Rapid identification of the misconfiguration by Ethan Brooks.  
- Swift rollback to a known good configuration.  
- Deployment of an automated health‑check script and alerting rule within the same incident window.  

## What went poorly  

- Initial absence of a health‑check flag caused traffic to be routed to an unhealthy instance.  
- No pre‑incident monitoring or alerting for load balancer health‑check failures.  

## Action items  

- [ ] @Ethan Brooks: Implement health‑check flag in all load balancer configurations — by 2023-02-15 [P1]  
- [ ] @Daniel Kim: Deploy automated health‑check script to all instances — by 2023-02-20 [P1]  
- [ ] @Ops Team: Add alerting rule for load balancer health‑check failures, ensuring notification within 5 minutes — by 2023-02-18 [P1]  
- [ ] @QA Team: Review and update load balancer configuration documentation — by 2023-02-28 [P2]  

## Lessons learned  
This incident highlighted the critical importance of enforcing health‑check flags on load balancers and maintaining automated health‑check scripts. Proactive monitoring and alerting are essential to detect and remediate such misconfigurations before they impact customers.

**Incident date:** 2023-10-12  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Authors:** Ethan Brooks (DevOps Engineer), Daniel Kim (Platform Engineer)  
**Status:** Final  

## Summary

On 12 Oct 2023 a 3‑hour outage of our public API was caused by a mis‑configured load balancer that failed to route traffic correctly. The outage impacted all mid‑market freight‑forwarding customers using our API for shipment tracking and rate calculations. The incident was detected by our monitoring system, escalated to the on‑call team, and resolved after traffic was rerouted and the load balancer was re‑configured.

## Timeline

- **09:00** – Monitoring alerts triggered: API latency spiked, error rate > 5 %.  
- **09:05** – On‑call engineer (Ethan) acknowledged alert, began diagnostics.  
- **09:15** – Incident escalated to platform team; Daniel joined.  
- **09:30** – Initial hypothesis: load balancer mis‑routing.

- **11:00** – API metrics returned to normal; error rate dropped to 0 %.  
- **12:00** – Incident closed; post‑mortem drafted.  

## Root cause

The root cause was a mis‑configured load balancer that was pointing to an outdated backend pool. The mis‑configuration caused the load balancer to route all traffic to a set of instances that were not serving the API, leading to a complete service outage. The mis‑configuration was introduced during a recent deployment of the load‑balancing layer, but no automated health checks or configuration validation were in place to catch the error before it impacted production.

## Contributing factors

- Lack of automated health checks on the load balancer configuration.  
- No configuration validation pipeline to detect incorrect backend pools.  
- Absence of a monitoring alert for mis‑configurations in the load balancer.  
- Limited visibility into the load balancer’s state during the incident.

- Rapid detection through existing latency and error‑rate alerts.  
- Clear communication between on‑call and platform teams.  
- Quick identification of the mis‑configuration and manual traffic rerouting.  
- Thorough documentation of the incident and root cause.  

## What went poorly

- The mis‑configuration was not caught by automated checks.  
- No alert existed for load balancer mis‑configurations, delaying detection.  
- The incident lasted 3 hours, impacting customers more than necessary.

# Postmortem: Retrospective Correction of 2023‑10‑12 API Outage Root Cause — 2024‑05‑20

**Incident date:** 2024‑05‑20  
**Severity:** SEV‑1 (high impact to internal reporting)  
**Authors:** Rajesh Kumar (P‑0005), Maya Patel (P‑0001)  
**Status:** Final  

## Summary  
On 2024‑05‑20 we amended the incident report for the 2023‑10‑12 API outage to correct the root‑cause attribution. Previously we believed a mis‑configured load balancer caused the outage; we now understand that a database schema change introduced a breaking change that was not caught by automated tests. The correction was approved by Maya Patel and Rajesh Kumar and updated across all internal documentation.

## Timeline  

- **09:00** – Maya Patel identifies a discrepancy between the 2023‑10‑12 post‑mortem and recent audit logs.  
- **09:15** – Rajesh Kumar pulls the database migration history and discovers a schema change applied on 2023‑10‑10 that removed a required column.  
- **09:30** – Investigation reveals the change was not covered by automated tests and caused the API outage.  
- **10:00** – Rajesh drafts a correction note and shares it with the incident response team.  
- **10:15** – Team reviews the evidence; consensus that the load balancer was not the root cause.  
- **10:30** – Maya Patel and Rajesh Kumar approve the correction.  
- **10:45** – Incident report for 2023‑10‑12 is updated in Confluence and the internal wiki.  
- **11:00** – Updated documentation is communicated to all stakeholders via Slack.  

## Root cause  
The root cause of the 2023‑10‑12 API outage was a database schema change that removed a column required by the API layer. The change was introduced on 2023‑10‑10 and deployed without automated regression tests covering the affected schema. Consequently, the API layer attempted to read the missing column, leading to a cascade of failures that lasted approximately three hours.

## Contributing factors  

- Lack of automated tests for database schema migrations.  
- No pre‑deployment validation step for schema changes.  
- Insufficient documentation of schema evolution in the incident response playbooks.  

## What went well  

- Rapid identification of the discrepancy by Maya Patel.  
- Clear evidence gathering and consensus building before approving the correction.  
- Transparent communication of the updated root cause to all stakeholders.  

## What went poorly  

- Initial misattribution to a load balancer mis‑configuration, which delayed the correct diagnosis.  
- Absence of automated checks for schema changes allowed the breaking change to go unnoticed.  

## Action items  

- [ ] @Rajesh Kumar: Implement automated schema migration tests in the CI pipeline — by 2024‑06‑15 [P1]  
- [ ] @Maya Patel: Update the incident response playbook to include a schema change validation step — by 2024‑06‑01 [P1]  
- [ ] @Engineering Lead: Conduct a quarterly review of all database migrations for test coverage gaps — by 2024‑07‑01 [P2]  

## Lessons learned  
This correction underscores the importance of rigorous testing for database schema changes. By embedding schema validation into our CI/CD process and updating our incident response playbooks, we can prevent similar misattributions and ensure faster, more accurate root‑cause analysis in the future.

- **09:35** — Service health checks returned to normal; 99.9 % uptime achieved.  
- **09:40** — Incident closed; post‑mortem drafted.  

## Root cause

The root cause was a misconfigured routing rule in the load balancer that directed traffic to an unavailable backend instance. The rule was inadvertently altered during a routine update, and the change was not validated against our automated configuration checks. As a result, the Order Processing service received no traffic, leading to the observed outage.

## Contributing factors

- Lack of automated validation for load balancer configuration changes.  
- No canary deployment or staged rollout for routing rule updates.  
- Insufficient monitoring of routing table integrity.  

## What went well

- Rapid detection through automated alerts.  
- Clear communication and quick decision‑making between Ethan and Daniel.  
- Successful rollback and hotfix deployment within 15 minutes.  

## What went poorly

- The misconfiguration slipped through manual review.  
- No automated guardrails prevented the faulty rule from being applied.  

## Action items

- [ ] @Daniel: Review and update the change‑management process to include canary deployments for routing changes — by 2023-06-15 [P2]  
- [ ] @OpsTeam: Add monitoring for routing table integrity and alert on anomalies — by 2023-06-10 [P1]  

## Lessons learned

We learned that even a single misconfigured routing rule can bring an entire service offline. By adding automated validation, canary testing, and tighter monitoring, we can catch such issues before they affect customers.  

Deploying now. Let me know if you spot any issues. Thanks for the support.

An S3 bucket that stores customer contact data was misconfigured to be publicly readable. The exposure was detected when Ethan Brooks noticed anomalous traffic patterns and reported it immediately. The incident was contained within 2 hours after isolation and patching.

# Postmortem: Misconfigured Load Balancer Outage — 2023-02-10

**Incident date:** 2023-02-03  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Authors:** Daniel Kim, Ethan Brooks  
**Status:** Final  

## Summary  
On February 3rd, a misconfigured load balancer caused traffic to be routed to an unhealthy instance, resulting in a brief service outage for several mid‑market freight‑forwarding customers. The outage lasted approximately 30 minutes and impacted API availability. The Ops team was notified within minutes of the failure, and the incident was resolved by rolling back to the previous stable configuration, applying the corrected settings, and deploying an automated health‑check script.

## Timeline  

- **09:00** — Load balancer health‑check flag missing; traffic routed to unhealthy instance.  
- **09:05** — Ops team alerted via existing monitoring; incident opened in Jira.  
- **09:10** — Ethan Brooks identifies misconfiguration in load balancer settings.  
- **09:15** — Rollback to previous stable configuration performed.  
- **09:20** — Corrected load balancer settings applied.  
- **09:25** — Automated health‑check script deployed to monitor instance health.  
- **09:30** — New alerting rule added to notify Ops within 5 minutes of similar failure.  
- **09:35** — Service restored; API availability confirmed.  
- **09:40** — Incident closed in Jira; postmortem drafted.  

## Root cause  
The root cause was a missing health‑check flag in the load balancer configuration. Without this flag, the load balancer could not detect that the instance was unhealthy and continued to route traffic to it, leading to the outage. The absence of an automated health‑check script and an alerting rule further delayed detection and response.

## Contributing factors  

- Lack of automated health‑check script prior to the incident.  
- No alerting rule for load balancer health‑check failures.  
- Insufficient documentation of load balancer configuration requirements.  

## What went well  

- Rapid identification of the misconfiguration by Ethan Brooks.  
- Swift rollback to a known good configuration.  
- Deployment of an automated health‑check script and alerting rule within the same incident window.  

## What went poorly  

- Initial absence of a health‑check flag caused traffic to be routed to an unhealthy instance.  
- No pre‑incident monitoring or alerting for load balancer health‑check failures.  

## Action items  

- [ ] @Ethan Brooks: Implement health‑check flag in all load balancer configurations — by 2023-02-15 [P1]  
- [ ] @Daniel Kim: Deploy automated health‑check script to all instances — by 2023-02-20 [P1]  
- [ ] @Ops Team: Add alerting rule for load balancer health‑check failures, ensuring notification within 5 minutes — by 2023-02-18 [P1]  
- [ ] @QA Team: Review and update load balancer configuration documentation — by 2023-02-28 [P2]  

## Lessons learned  
This incident highlighted the critical importance of enforcing health‑check flags on load balancers and maintaining automated health‑check scripts. Proactive monitoring and alerting are essential to detect and remediate such misconfigurations before they impact customers.

Let me know if anything breaks.

On 12 Oct 2023 a 3‑hour outage of our public API was caused by a mis‑configured load balancer that failed to route traffic correctly. The outage impacted all mid‑market freight‑forwarding customers using our API for shipment tracking and rate calculations. The incident was detected by our monitoring system, escalated to the on‑call team, and resolved after traffic was rerouted and the load balancer was re‑configured.

# Postmortem: Load Balancer Routing Misconfiguration — 2023-05-12

**Incident date:** 2023-05-05  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Authors:** Ethan Brooks, Daniel Kim  
**Status:** Draft  

## Summary

On May 5th, a misconfigured routing rule in our load balancer caused the Order Processing service to become unreachable. The outage impacted all inbound order traffic, leading to a temporary loss of service for our mid‑market freight‑forwarding customers. Within 15 minutes of detection, we rolled back to the last stable configuration and applied a hotfix, restoring 99.9 % uptime within 30 minutes.

## Timeline

- **09:00** — Monitoring alerts flagged a spike in 5xx errors from the Order Processing service.  
- **09:02** — Ethan Brooks identified the load balancer as the source of the issue.  
- **09:04** — Daniel Kim approved an immediate rollback to the previous stable configuration.  
- **09:05** — Rollback initiated; traffic was redirected to the stable backend pool.  
- **09:10** — Hotfix deployment began; updated routing rule pushed to the load balancer.  
- **09:25** — Configuration applied successfully; traffic routing restored.  
- **09:35** — Service health checks returned to normal; 99.9 % uptime achieved.  
- **09:40** — Incident closed; post‑mortem drafted.  

## Root cause

The root cause was a misconfigured routing rule in the load balancer that directed traffic to an unavailable backend instance. The rule was inadvertently altered during a routine update, and the change was not validated against our automated configuration checks. As a result, the Order Processing service received no traffic, leading to the observed outage.

## Contributing factors

- Lack of automated validation for load balancer configuration changes.  
- No canary deployment or staged rollout for routing rule updates.  
- Insufficient monitoring of routing table integrity.  

## What went well

- Rapid detection through automated alerts.  
- Clear communication and quick decision‑making between Ethan and Daniel.  
- Successful rollback and hotfix deployment within 15 minutes.  

## What went poorly

- The misconfiguration slipped through manual review.  
- No automated guardrails prevented the faulty rule from being applied.  

## Action items

- [ ] @Ethan: Implement automated validation scripts for load balancer configs — by 2023-06-01 [P1]  
- [ ] @Daniel: Review and update the change‑management process to include canary deployments for routing changes — by 2023-06-15 [P2]  
- [ ] @OpsTeam: Add monitoring for routing table integrity and alert on anomalies — by 2023-06-10 [P1]  

## Lessons learned

We learned that even a single misconfigured routing rule can bring an entire service offline. By adding automated validation, canary testing, and tighter monitoring, we can catch such issues before they affect customers.  

Deploying now. Let me know if you spot any issues. Thanks for the support.

# Postmortem: Retrospective Correction of 2023‑10‑12 API Outage Root Cause — 2024‑05‑20

**Incident date:** 2024‑05‑20  
**Severity:** SEV‑1 (high impact to internal reporting)  
**Authors:** Rajesh Kumar (P‑0005), Maya Patel (P‑0001)  
**Status:** Final  

## Summary  
On 2024‑05‑20 we amended the incident report for the 2023‑10‑12 API outage to correct the root‑cause attribution. Previously we believed a mis‑configured load balancer caused the outage; we now understand that a database schema change introduced a breaking change that was not caught by automated tests. The correction was approved by Maya Patel and Rajesh Kumar and updated across all internal documentation.

## Timeline  

- **09:00** – Maya Patel identifies a discrepancy between the 2023‑10‑12 post‑mortem and recent audit logs.  
- **09:15** – Rajesh Kumar pulls the database migration history and discovers a schema change applied on 2023‑10‑10 that removed a required column.  
- **09:30** – Investigation reveals the change was not covered by automated tests and caused the API outage.  
- **10:00** – Rajesh drafts a correction note and shares it with the incident response team.  
- **10:15** – Team reviews the evidence; consensus that the load balancer was not the root cause.  
- **10:30** – Maya Patel and Rajesh Kumar approve the correction.  
- **10:45** – Incident report for 2023‑10‑12 is updated in Confluence and the internal wiki.  
- **11:00** – Updated documentation is communicated to all stakeholders via Slack.  

## Root cause  
The root cause of the 2023‑10‑12 API outage was a database schema change that removed a column required by the API layer. The change was introduced on 2023‑10‑10 and deployed without automated regression tests covering the affected schema. Consequently, the API layer attempted to read the missing column, leading to a cascade of failures that lasted approximately three hours.

## Contributing factors  

- Lack of automated tests for database schema migrations.  
- No pre‑deployment validation step for schema changes.  
- Insufficient documentation of schema evolution in the incident response playbooks.  

## What went well  

- Rapid identification of the discrepancy by Maya Patel.  
- Clear evidence gathering and consensus building before approving the correction.  
- Transparent communication of the updated root cause to all stakeholders.  

## What went poorly  

- Initial misattribution to a load balancer mis‑configuration, which delayed the correct diagnosis.  
- Absence of automated checks for schema changes allowed the breaking change to go unnoticed.  

## Action items  

- [ ] @Rajesh Kumar: Implement automated schema migration tests in the CI pipeline — by 2024‑06‑15 [P1]  
- [ ] @Maya Patel: Update the incident response playbook to include a schema change validation step — by 2024‑06‑01 [P1]  
- [ ] @Engineering Lead: Conduct a quarterly review of all database migrations for test coverage gaps — by 2024‑07‑01 [P2]  

## Lessons learned  
This correction underscores the importance of rigorous testing for database schema changes. By embedding schema validation into our CI/CD process and updating our incident response playbooks, we can prevent similar misattributions and ensure faster, more accurate root‑cause analysis in the future.

## Current Belief About the 2023-11-15 Sales Portal Outage

**As of now (post-June 2024), the system believes:**
The root cause of the 2023-11-15 sales portal outage was a **misconfigured firewall rule**, not merely a misconfigured load-balancer rule as originally documented. Per the retrospective note in ART-EV-2024-154-002: *"We now understand that the root cause was a mis-configured firewall rule that was not captured in the original documentation."* Maya Patel and the CTO reviewed audit findings and approved corrections to the incident documentation, the knowledge graph entry, and the firewall rule change process (adding automated validation and a new monitoring rule).

**When the system first learned the original account:**
2023-11-15 — the incident records (ART-EV-2023-126-001 and ART-EV-2023-126-002) documented the load-balancer mis-configuration as the sole cause on that date.

**When the system incorporated the corrected version:**
2024-06-15 — the retrospective audit note in ART-EV-2024-154-002 formally corrected the account. ART-EV-2023-126-001 also cross-references this correction: *"(retroactively_corrected_by) See retrospective audit (ART-EV-2024-154-001)."*

---

## What the System Would Have Said on 2023-12-01

On 2023-12-01, the correction had not yet been made (it occurred in June 2024). The system would have answered:

# Postmortem: Retrospective Correction of 2023‑10‑12 API Outage Root Cause — 2024‑05‑20

**Incident date:** 2024‑05‑20  
**Severity:** SEV‑1 (high impact to internal reporting)  
**Authors:** Rajesh Kumar (P‑0005), Maya Patel (P‑0001)  
**Status:** Final  

## Summary  
On 2024‑05‑20 we amended the incident report for the 2023‑10‑12 API outage to correct the root‑cause attribution. Previously we believed a mis‑configured load balancer caused the outage; we now understand that a database schema change introduced a breaking change that was not caught by automated tests. The correction was approved by Maya Patel and Rajesh Kumar and updated across all internal documentation.

## Timeline  

- **09:00** – Maya Patel identifies a discrepancy between the 2023‑10‑12 post‑mortem and recent audit logs.  
- **09:15** – Rajesh Kumar pulls the database migration history and discovers a schema change applied on 2023‑10‑10 that removed a required column.  
- **09:30** – Investigation reveals the change was not covered by automated tests and caused the API outage.  
- **10:00** – Rajesh drafts a correction note and shares it with the incident response team.  
- **10:15** – Team reviews the evidence; consensus that the load balancer was not the root cause.  
- **10:30** – Maya Patel and Rajesh Kumar approve the correction.  
- **10:45** – Incident report for 2023‑10‑12 is updated in Confluence and the internal wiki.  
- **11:00** – Updated documentation is communicated to all stakeholders via Slack.  

## Root cause  
The root cause of the 2023‑10‑12 API outage was a database schema change that removed a column required by the API layer. The change was introduced on 2023‑10‑10 and deployed without automated regression tests covering the affected schema. Consequently, the API layer attempted to read the missing column, leading to a cascade of failures that lasted approximately three hours.

## Contributing factors  

- Lack of automated tests for database schema migrations.  
- No pre‑deployment validation step for schema changes.  
- Insufficient documentation of schema evolution in the incident response playbooks.  

## What went well  

- Rapid identification of the discrepancy by Maya Patel.  
- Clear evidence gathering and consensus building before approving the correction.  
- Transparent communication of the updated root cause to all stakeholders.  

## What went poorly  

- Initial misattribution to a load balancer mis‑configuration, which delayed the correct diagnosis.  
- Absence of automated checks for schema changes allowed the breaking change to go unnoticed.  

## Action items  

- [ ] @Rajesh Kumar: Implement automated schema migration tests in the CI pipeline — by 2024‑06‑15 [P1]  
- [ ] @Maya Patel: Update the incident response playbook to include a schema change validation step — by 2024‑06‑01 [P1]  
- [ ] @Engineering Lead: Conduct a quarterly review of all database migrations for test coverage gaps — by 2024‑07‑01 [P2]  

## Lessons learned  
This correction underscores the importance of rigorous testing for database schema changes. By embedding schema validation into our CI/CD process and updating our incident response playbooks, we can prevent similar misattributions and ensure faster, more accurate root‑cause analysis in the future.

# Postmortem: Load Balancer Routing Misconfiguration — 2023-05-12

**Incident date:** 2023-05-05  
**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Authors:** Ethan Brooks, Daniel Kim  
**Status:** Draft  

## Summary

On May 5th, a misconfigured routing rule in our load balancer caused the Order Processing service to become unreachable. The outage impacted all inbound order traffic, leading to a temporary loss of service for our mid‑market freight‑forwarding customers. Within 15 minutes of detection, we rolled back to the last stable configuration and applied a hotfix, restoring 99.9 % uptime within 30 minutes.

## Timeline

- **09:00** — Monitoring alerts flagged a spike in 5xx errors from the Order Processing service.  
- **09:02** — Ethan Brooks identified the load balancer as the source of the issue.  
- **09:04** — Daniel Kim approved an immediate rollback to the previous stable configuration.  
- **09:05** — Rollback initiated; traffic was redirected to the stable backend pool.  
- **09:10** — Hotfix deployment began; updated routing rule pushed to the load balancer.  
- **09:25** — Configuration applied successfully; traffic routing restored.  
- **09:35** — Service health checks returned to normal; 99.9 % uptime achieved.  
- **09:40** — Incident closed; post‑mortem drafted.  

## Root cause

The root cause was a misconfigured routing rule in the load balancer that directed traffic to an unavailable backend instance. The rule was inadvertently altered during a routine update, and the change was not validated against our automated configuration checks. As a result, the Order Processing service received no traffic, leading to the observed outage.

## Contributing factors

- Lack of automated validation for load balancer configuration changes.  
- No canary deployment or staged rollout for routing rule updates.  
- Insufficient monitoring of routing table integrity.  

## What went well

- Rapid detection through automated alerts.  
- Clear communication and quick decision‑making between Ethan and Daniel.  
- Successful rollback and hotfix deployment within 15 minutes.  

## What went poorly

- The misconfiguration slipped through manual review.  
- No automated guardrails prevented the faulty rule from being applied.  

## Action items

- [ ] @Ethan: Implement automated validation scripts for load balancer configs — by 2023-06-01 [P1]  
- [ ] @Daniel: Review and update the change‑management process to include canary deployments for routing changes — by 2023-06-15 [P2]  
- [ ] @OpsTeam: Add monitoring for routing table integrity and alert on anomalies — by 2023-06-10 [P1]  

## Lessons learned

We learned that even a single misconfigured routing rule can bring an entire service offline. By adding automated validation, canary testing, and tighter monitoring, we can catch such issues before they affect customers.  

Deploying now. Let me know if you spot any issues. Thanks for the support.
